results.title: KIP-1323: Initialization of share group offsets from a specific offset or a file

storage.value:
Status

Current state: Accepted

Discussion thread: here

Voting thread: here

JIRA: here

Please keep the discussion on the mailing list rather than commenting on the wiki (wiki discussions get unwieldy fast).

Motivation

introduced share groups and included the kafka-share-groups.sh  tool for initializing and resetting the share-partition start offsets. This was inspired by the equivalent kafka-consumer-groups.sh  tool for consumer groups, but it did not include all of the options for resetting options which are available for consumer groups.

When users are migrating from a consumer group to a share group, it is natural that they would want to initialize the share group with the committed offsets from the consumer group. Programmatically, this is easy, but there is no way using kafka-share-groups.sh  to achieve this. This KIP adds extra options to that tool to make this kind of migration easy.

Proposed Changes

Additional options are added to kafka-share-groups.sh  to give more flexibility for initialization of share group offsets. These options match those which exist in kafka-consumer-groups.sh .

First, --to-offset lets the user specify a specific offset. For example, the following command will set the SPSO for share group SG1 topic T1 partition 0 to offset 1234.

$ bin/kafka-share-groups.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --reset-offsets --group SG1 --topic T1:0 --to-offset 1234 --execute 

If the specified offset is lower than the earliest offset, it is reset to the earliest offset. If the specified offset is higher than the latest offset, it is reset to the latest offset. This is the same behavior as kafka-consumer-groups.sh .

Second, --from-file  lets the user provide a CSV file containing lines topic,partition,offset  to specify the topic names, partitions and offsets to reset. This makes the following migration from a consumer group to a share group possible.

$ bin/kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --reset-offsets --group CG1 --all-topics --to-current --export --dry-run > FILENAME 

$ bin/kafka-share-groups.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --reset-offsets --group SG1 --from-file FILENAME --execute 

It is possible to export the offset information for multiple consumer groups together with kafka-consumer-groups.sh , and the resulting file contains 4 columns (group ID, topic name, partition, offset). If such a file is used to reset the offsets for a share group, the offset information is filtered by the group ID. Again, this is the same behavior as kafka-consumer-groups.sh .

It is probably more useful to export the offset information for a single consumer group, and then the resulting file contains 3 columns (topic name, partition, offset). If such a file is used to reset the offsets for a share group, the group ID of the share group could be the same as the consumer group (it will be necessary to delete the consumer group so the group ID can be used by the share group), or the group ID of the share group could be different.

The kafka-share-groups.sh  tool is only able to export the offset information for one group at a time. The --reset-offsets  option only supports one group at a time and this KIP does not change that restriction.

In order to facilitate migration in the other direction, or from one share group to another, the --export  option is provided, along with --to-current . The purpose of --to-current  is to export the current offsets, as opposed to the earliest or latest offsets.

$ bin/kafka-share-groups.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --reset-offsets --group SG1 --all-topics --to-current --export --dry-run > FILENAME

$ bin/kafka-share-groups.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --reset-offsets --group SG2 --from-file FILENAME --execute 

Public Interfaces

Command-line tools

kafka-share-groups.sh

The following new options are added to this tool.

OptionDescription
--exportExport offset information in CSV format. Supported options: reset-offsets.
--from-file <String: path to CSV file>Reset offsets to values defined in CSV file.
--to-currentReset offsets to current offset.
--to-offset <Long: offset>Reset offsets to a specific offset.

Compatibility, Deprecation, and Migration Plan

New options are added to an existing tool. The underlying admin APIs are unchanged and the options will work with Apache Kafka 4.2 and later.

Test Plan

Unit tests will be written to test the new options.

Rejected Alternatives

None

results.title: KIP-1324: Support client configuration observability

storage.value:
Status

Current state: Under discussion

Discussion thread: here

JIRA: here

Please keep the discussion on the mailing list rather than commenting on the wiki (wiki discussions get unwieldy fast).

Motivation

The teams that operate a Kafka cluster have no direct way to see how the clients connected to it are configured. In many organizations, the teams developing and deploying client applications are separate and intentionally siloed from the teams that manage the cluster (the most extreme case being management via a hosted service). As a result, an operator investigating a problem has to get the configuration from each application team, which delays the diagnosis and troubleshooting.

The gap matters because client configuration is a common source of problems. The large number of available configuration options bewilders teams new to the ecosystem, and even accomplished teams are not immune to the occasional misconfiguration. The gap impact gets more noticeable as Kafka’s usage increases within organizations, so centralized observability of client configuration becomes increasingly critical. 

This KIP takes the first step in closing this gap by introducing a standard interface by which a cluster asks its clients for built-in configurations. Each client instance pushes the requested keys once, as soon as it discovers a broker advertising the feature, and the cluster hands that configuration to an operator-supplied plugin. The cluster decides what is collected, so an operator can start with a handful of keys and widen the set as confidence grows. 

At the moment, some client configuration already reaches the brokers, but only inside individual requests: client.id and the client software name and version arrive with every connection, a few producer settings are visible in Produce requests, and a few consumer and group settings in group heartbeats. These are scattered values, consumed within the scope of each request on whichever broker serves it, not recorded or tied to the client instance or framework behind them, so nothing can expose them as one client's configuration. Most configurations that are key in understanding and troubleshooting application behaviour never appear in any request at all. This KIP closes these gaps with one snapshot per client instance, carrying the identifiers needed to group it.

This KIP covers both the clients and the frameworks that embed them. Client snapshots alone do not describe an application such as Kafka Streams, which has settings of its own (num.stream.threads, processing.guarantee, num.standby.replicas). So every client (producer, consumer, share consumer, admin) pushes its own snapshot, a framework can push one snapshot of its own configuration through one of its clients (Kafka Streams does it with this KIP), and the framework identifiers from KIP-1368 let a plugin group every snapshot of one application instance.

The mechanism is opt-in on the broker and opt-out on the client. Nothing is advertised until an operator configures a plugin. What is collected is a default set of built-in keys, which the operator narrows or widens by name. A change reaches only clients that run their exchange after it, so running clients pick it up at their next restart.

It is strongly advised that this KIP is implemented and made the default in all Kafka client libraries, so that an operator gets visibility by configuring the cluster alone, without changes to applications. 

This KIP delivers a one-time view of each client instance's configuration. A change to a client's configuration means a new client instance, which reports again. It delivers the hooks end to end: clients push what the cluster requests, the plugin acts on each snapshot and can give feedback on it, and the client reacts to that feedback as the cluster instructs. The cluster controls both: what is observed (requested keys), and how a client application reacts when the plugin rejects its snapshot (validation with modes: by default the application logs the cluster's feedback and keeps running. An operator can instead have it fail before performing any operation). No validation rule ships with this KIP, the hooks do, together with the client behaviour that handles their outcome. Overriding client configurations, and asking running clients to report again, are out of scope for now.

Public Interfaces

This KIP adds two RPCs, so that clients can send the configurations the cluster requests (keys and values), and a broker plugin interface, ClientConfigsPlugin, that receives them and can give feedback:

  • GetClientConfigsSubscription : the client sends it to ask the cluster which configuration keys it requests. The response tells the client whether it must wait to push and get the cluster's feedback before its first operation.
  • PushClientConfigs : the client sends the values of the requested keys, once per client snapshot. The response carries the cluster's feedback and how the client application must handle it (e.g., log violations and keep running, or fail)

The KIP also adds:

  • broker and client configurations
  • one new error code (and reuses POLICY_VIOLATION)
  • broker metrics
  • one public client method for frameworks such as Kafka Streams
  • a broker configuration client.configs.validation.mode, public enum ValidationMode,
    • this represents a config validation mode by which the operator decides how client applications react to the plugin outcome (e.g., snapshots for which the plugin may throw PolicyViolationException, see "Client Behaviour, Validation". No validation rule ships with this KIP
  • a ClientType field in PushClientConfigs, to be able to tell which client (e.g., producer, consumer, admin, share consumer), or which framework (e.g., streams), a snapshot describes

Definitions

Client Instance ID

KIP-714 introduced it as a UUID that identifies one client instance for telemetry, and KIP-1313 makes it available for all paths: the client generates it at construction and sends it in request header version 3, which both new RPCs use. 

This KIP builds on top of

  • KIP-1313 (accepted) for the client instance id: both new RPCs introduced in this KIP use request header version 3, and the broker takes the client instance id that KIP-1313 associates with the request. A request whose header carries no valid client instance id (e.g., client library that does not follow KIP-1313) is rejected with INVALID_REQUEST.
  • KIP-1368 for the framework name, version and id in the plugin context. Given that KIP-1368 is still under discussion at the moment, we consider the alternative that without KIP-1368 those accessors return empty, and the impact is simply that a plugin cannot group the snapshots of one Kafka Streams instance.  Everything else in this KIP works as designed (the improved grouping capability could land independently).

The accessors are listed under ClientConfigs, ClientConfigEntry and ClientConfigsContext below.

Configurations sent

A key is pushed when the cluster asks for it and the client is willing to send it. The cluster asks through the broker configuration client.configs.requested.keys. The client decides whether to send the config based on 2 main categories:

  • Sensitive configs
    • never sent by a client, even if requested by the broker. This filter is hardcoded.
    • it includes:
      • any key of type PASSWORD in Kafka's existing ConfigDef.Type
      • any key in the sasl., ssl. or security. families (as a prefix, or an infix such as producer.ssl.)
      • bootstrap.servers and bootstrap.controllers
  • Built-in non-sensitive configs
    • sent if requested by the broker and not explicitly denied by the client (not matched by the client deny list configs.push.denied.keys)
    • it includes every key defined in the client's own configuration definition (ProducerConfig, ConsumerConfig, AdminClientConfig, StreamsConfig, ShareConsumerConfig), including Type.CLASS keys

Other considerations:

  • requested keys the client does not define are ignored by the client, so custom configs (keys in the client's configuration that it does not define, e.g., settings read by a serializer, interceptor or the application itself) are never sent in this KIP. The same applies to keys a client defines but does not support for its type or group protocol (e.g., session.timeout.ms defined for the consumer but not supported under the consumer group protocol, so a consumer using that group.protocol ignores it).
    • if a client sends a key it does not define anyway, the entry is typed UNKNOWN and the broker drops it before invoking the plugin (see Broker Behaviour).
  • requested keys are pushed whether or not they hold the default value
    • each entry carries a Source field telling whether the key was set in the client's configuration or keeps the client's default
    • knowing the Source lets a plugin tell what an application changed from what it inherited (without knowing the defaults of every client library and version). It also gives a later enforcement KIP a place to mark values the broker applied (e.g., value 2 used in the future to tell that the config is "broker-enforced").
  • sensitive keys are filtered before any value is rendered. On top of that, the deny list supports prefixes to easily reduce what is sent
  • if nothing remains after filtering, the client still sends a push with no entries, so that a plugin can tell a client with nothing to send from one that never reported
  • class-name keys (key.serializer, value.deserializer, partitioner.class, interceptor.classes, partition.assignment.strategy, metric.reporters and similar) are built-in non-sensitive configs:
    • when requested, the client pushes the fully qualified class names it is configured with, whether set by name or passed to the constructor;
    • they reveal the application's package naming and its choice of serializers, interceptors or partitioners, not credentials, endpoints or data, and they are among the most common root causes in client support cases
    • none is in the default set, so they flow only when an operator requests them
    • an application that prefers not to send them lists them in configs.push.denied.keys
    • key names and the sensitive-config rules are the client library's own
      • the default requested set uses the Java client's names
      • a library whose names differ ignores names it does not define, and a library with a different naming convention adjusts its sensitive-config rules accordingly
  • a few keys describe the environment rather than behaviour: client.rack and, in Kafka Streams, application.server and state.dir. They are not sensitive configs filtered out by default, so an operator can request them by name (client.rack included in the default requested set). An application that prefers not to send them can exclude them by adding them to configs.push.denied.keys.

Default Configuration for Apache Kafka clients

The default value for the broker configuration client.configs.requested.keys  is one list for all client types. It includes:

  • identity keys that let a plugin group snapshots by application, consumer group, transactional producer or Streams application (client.id, group.id, group.instance.id, transactional.id, application.id)
  • client specific configs (all merged in a single list, defining the set of configs the broker/operator wants to "observe" from its clients, consumers, share consumers, producers and admins)
  • the list contains no class names and no custom keys

This is the full list of default properties requested by the broker.

Operators widen or narrow this list by name. New client configurations are added to the default in a later release (or kept out and operators can still add them by name).

Client Configuration Plugins

This KIP introduces a new broker-side interface named ClientConfigsPlugin.

  • includes a single hook onClientConfigs
  • invoked synchronously with each snapshot the broker accepted (see Broker Behaviour)
    • each implementation can take any desired action on the received config snapshot: log, validate, forward it, store it, etc. 
    • the implementation should return "quickly", running lightweight, in-memory work synchronously (e.g., validations), and offload heavier work asynchronously (e.g, forwarding, storage)
  • it may reject the snapshot by throwing PolicyViolationException
    • the client receives the error in the response, and how the client application reacts is the cluster's decision via the broker config client.configs.validation.mode (see Configuration -> Broker)
  • operators install an implementation through the broker configuration described later
  • no implementation ships with this KIP (neither for observing nor for validating)
    • the KIP delivers the hooks and the client behaviour that handles their outcome
  • each snapshot reaches only the broker the client sent it to (or, after a retry, also the broker it retried on). The plugin stores it according to its needs, e.g., in a shared place such as a topic or an external store for a cluster-wide view
  • the plugin is not told when a client instance closes or restarts. A restarted client pushes again under a new client instance id. Some pushed identifiers can help a plugin link a snapshot to the same client after a restart, and expire the previous one: transactional.id and group.instance.id (default requested set), the KIP-1368 framework id for Kafka Streams, or client.id where the application keeps it unique per instance. Without one of these, old snapshots can only be expired by age

End-to-end flow

The following sequence diagram shows the interaction between the different components:


The flow includes the following steps:

  1. The client establishes a connection to the broker and sends an ApiVersions request
  2. If client.configs.plugin.class  is configured, the broker advertises GetClientConfigsSubscription  and PushClientConfigs  in the ApiVersions response
  3. From its network thread, the client sends a GetClientConfigsSubscription request to the least-loaded node that supports both RPCs
  4. GetClientConfigsSubscription response carries the keys the cluster requests and the broker's validation mode (Mode)
  5. If anything is requested, the client collects those keys (see "Configurations sent"), builds a PushClientConfigs request (with no entries if none survives the filtering) and sends it
  6. The broker checks the push (e.g., size), drops the entries the cluster did not request and any typed UNKNOWN, and calls ClientConfigsPlugin.onClientConfigs(), which returns to accept the snapshot or throws PolicyViolationException to reject it
  7. The broker returns the PushClientConfigs response as soon as the call returned or threw: ErrorCode NONE, or POLICY_VIOLATION with the exception's message as ErrorMessage when the plugin rejected the snapshot, plus the Mode
  8. The client marks its exchange as complete for its lifetime. These steps run on the client's network thread (triggered from they client constructors), and never block the constructor. The client's first operation waits for the GetClientConfigsSubscription response and, in reject mode, for the PushClientConfigs response (see Client Behaviour, Validation)" 

ClientConfigs, ClientConfigEntry and ClientConfigsContext

When the broker receives a PushClientConfigs push, it builds a ClientConfigs snapshot from the requested entries and a ClientConfigsContext. The context carries the request context, the client id, the client instance id (KIP-1313), the client type that this KIP adds to the push request, the client software values (KIP-511) and framework values (KIP-1368) from ApiVersionsRequest, the connection's address, the broker's receive time and the validation mode in effect.

clientType() /** From ApiVersionsRequest, or "unknown" if not known. */ String clientSoftwareName(); String clientSoftwareVersion(); /** From ApiVersionsRequest (KIP-1368), if the client is embedded in a framework and sent them. */ Optional clientFrameworkName(); Optional clientFrameworkVersion(); Optional clientFrameworkId(); /** The client connection's source address and port, as seen by the broker. */ String clientSourceAddress(); int clientSourcePort(); /** The receiving broker's node id. */ int nodeId(); /** Broker time at which the request was received. */ long receivedTimeMs();    /** * The broker's client.configs.validation.mode when this push was handled: determines what the client does with a * PolicyViolationException thrown by onClientConfigs: WARN makes the clients log and keep running, * REJECT tells the client to fail. */ ValidationMode validationMode(); }]]>


entries) { } public record ClientConfigEntry(String name, String value, ConfigEntry.ConfigType type, Source source) { public enum Source { DEFAULT, // 0 USER; // 1 // 2 is reserved for a future broker-enforced source     } }]]>



ClientConfigsPlugin


No specific implementation ships with this KIP.

Exceptions

The broker checks the snapshot size before invoking the plugin. If it exceeds client.configs.max.bytes, it returns CLIENT_CONFIGS_TOO_LARGE with the limit in the error message. Other plugin failures are not reported to the client. A PolicyViolationException thrown by onClientConfigs is answered as POLICY_VIOLATION, reusing the existing error code and exception (no new exception is added)


Configuration

Broker

Configuration name

Description

Values

client.configs.plugin.class 

  • fully qualified name of a ClientConfigsPlugin implementation
  • when null the feature is off (RPCs not advertised in ApiVersionsResponse and requests for them are rejected)

Type: class

Default: null

static config (roll needed)

client.configs.max.bytes

  • maximum snapshot size the broker accepts: the serialized size of the Configs field of a PushClientConfigs request (the rest of the request is bounded by the ClientType length limit)
  • included in the error message when a snapshot is rejected for size

Type: int

Default: 10240 (10 KB)

static config (roll needed)

client.configs.requested.keys 

  • the configuration keys the cluster requests from every client
  • exact key names (no wildcard or prefix accepted, fail when config set)
  • a key the client does not define is ignored, and a sensitive key is filtered out by the client
  • empty means nothing is requested and clients send nothing
  • cluster-wide value; a client uses whatever the broker it asked returns.

Type: list

Default: see "Default Configuration for Apache Kafka clients"

dynamic config (no roll)

client.configs.validation.mode

  • determines how client applications react when the plugin rejects its snapshot (a PolicyViolationException)
  • values are:
    • warn: the client should log the feedback and keep running
    • reject: the client should fail before its first operation (see Client Behaviour, Validation)
  • cluster-wide value, carried as Mode in both responses
  • a change reaches only clients that run their exchange after it

Type: string (warn | reject)

Default: warn

dynamic config (no roll)

The plugin class and the size limit are static. The requested set and the validation mode are dynamic cluster-wide broker configurations (so they can change without a broker roll)

About rolls and restarts

  • enabling the feature is one broker roll (to set the plugin class) and no client restart. Every running client reconnects during the roll, sees the RPCs advertised for the first time, and runs its exchange.
  • a later change to the requested set is one command and no roll, but it reaches running clients only at their next restart (each client runs its exchange once). Operators should adjust the list before enabling the plugin.
  • setting the list empty stops collection with the same command and no roll: clients that start afterwards receive nothing and send nothing
  • changing the validation mode doesn't require a roll, and reaches clients that run their exchange afterwards: moving to reject does not re-evaluate running clients (a rejection they logged in warn mode applies at their next restart), and moving back to warn does not recover a client that already failed (needs restart)

Client

Applies to KafkaProducer, KafkaConsumer, KafkaShareConsumer and Admin clients, as well as Kafka Streams.

Configuration name

Description

Values

enable.configs.push

  • whether the client takes part in configuration collection: asks the cluster what it requests and pushes it
  • when false the client does not send any of the 2 config-related requests

Type: boolean

Default: true for producer, consumer, share consumer and Kafka Streams; false for the admin client

configs.push.denied.keys

Exact key names, or prefixes ending in ., that are never pushed even if requested

Type: list

Default: null

Notes:

  • proposing admin client default to false given that it's typically one-off operations, so for this common case each run would push a snapshot under a fresh client instance id (as opposed to producers and consumers that typically live as long as the application runs and carry the configuration operators want to see)
    • still, a long-running admin client can enable it (e.g. Kafka Streams does so for its own admin client)
  • no client-side allow-list: the cluster defines the keys it wants to observe from it's clients, operators can add/remove from that list, and the applications can only remove keys from that set. This is the initial approach as part of this KIP, future work could extend and add more client side flexibility if needed (e.g., to allow clients to push custom configs, out of scope for now)

Client API

One method is added to Admin, Producer, Consumer and ShareConsumer so that a framework can push its own configs through whichever client it embeds.

registerLogicalClientConfigs(String logicalClientType, AbstractConfig configs);]]>

Notes:

  • logicalClientType  becomes the push's ClientType . Implementations should pass the framework's name as KIP-1368 defines it, so a plugin can match the snapshot with the connection's framework name.
    • the framework id (KIP-1368) lets a plugin group the snapshot with the framework's other clients (e.g., the admin client, consumers and producers of the same Kafka Streams instance)
  • method to register is added to all four interfaces so that a framework can push through whichever client it embeds (same pattern used for registering metrics proposed by KIP-1076)
  • Kafka Streams uses it on its admin client to push the stream-specific configs through it

Protocol

GetClientConfigsSubscriptionRequest

The request has no specific fields in version 0. It uses request header version 3 (the headerVersions property KIP-1313 adds to request schemas), and the broker takes the client instance id from KIP-1313.


GetClientConfigsSubscriptionResponse



PushClientConfigsRequest

Notes:

  • after a GetClientConfigsSubscription response (that requests anything), the client sends one PushClientConfigsRequest per snapshot, from its network thread:
    • one push with its own configuration (ClientType set to its client type)
    • if a framework registered its configuration on this client, a second push with the framework's configuration (ClientType set to the framework name)
    • e.g., an admin client used by Kafka Streams would send 1 GetClientConfigsSubscription and 2 PushClientConfigsRequest (one with its own admin configs, one with the streams configs), or if Kafka Streams registers after the admin client's own exchange completed, a second exchange runs with 1 GetClientConfigsSubscription and 1 PushClientConfigsRequest to push the streams configs.
  • the exchange runs once per client instance (plus one more for a framework snapshot registered after it completed, see Client API)
  • the client retries only when no response arrives (see Client Behaviour), and any response ends that push
  • ClientType tells a plugin the type of client that the snapshot describes, and if it's the client's own configuration, or a framework's configuration pushed through the client.
    • reserved values, meaning the sending client's own configuration: producer, consumer, share-consumer, admin
    • any other value marks a framework snapshot and is the framework's name as KIP-1368 defines it (e.g., org.apache.kafka.streams)
    • null also means the sending client's own configuration, without saying which kind (for client libraries that do not distinguish client types). A library that does should use the reserved values
    • the Java clients always set it:
      • KafkaProducer sends producer, KafkaConsumer sends consumer (with either group.protocol), KafkaShareConsumer sends share-consumer, and the admin client sends admin
      • the admin client where Kafka Streams registers its configuration also sends a second snapshot with ClientType org.apache.kafka.streams 
    • the producers and consumers embedded in Kafka Streams and Kafka Connect send their own type (producer, consumer)
    • if not null: non-empty, at most 249 characters (same character rules as ClientSoftwareName in ApiVersionsRequest), otherwise the request fails with INVALID_REQUEST
  • Value is rendered as the Java client renders configuration values (ConfigDef.convertToString): LIST entries joined with a comma and no spaces, CLASS as the fully qualified class name, BOOLEAN as true or false, numbers in decimal, null when the value is null.
    • other client libraries should render values the same way, so a plugin reads a key the same whatever library sent it


PushClientConfigsResponse

ErrorMessage carries a brief reason for an error (e.g., on CLIENT_CONFIGS_TOO_LARGE it states the broker's limit. On POLICY_VIOLATION it is the plugin's message). This response is sent as soon as onClientConfigs returned or threw.

Errors

  • Both RPCs can return:
    • UNSUPPORTED_VERSION if the feature is off on the broker (no plugin configured), or the requested version is not supported
    • INVALID_REQUEST: if a request header has no valid client instance id (KIP-1313), or a malformed push (including a ClientType outside its format or length limit).
  • PushClientConfigs can additionally return:
    • CLIENT_CONFIGS_TOO_LARGE:
      • indicates that the snapshot size exceeds the broker's client.configs.max.bytes
      • ErrorMessage states the limit
      • checked before the plugin is invoked
      • added by this KIP with its exception ClientConfigsTooLargeException, not retriable
  • Client-side handling on any error:
    • log the broker's message once at WARN
    • end that push (no retry)
    • the client keeps operating normally and nothing reaches the application
    • only a missing response (timeout or disconnect) is retried, as described under Client Behaviour
  • plugin outcomes are not reported to the client, so there is no plugin error code
  • throttling applies to both RPCs through ThrottleTimeMs and is not an error
  • pushing configurations is performed on a best-effort basis. Failure to send the configuration should not prevent the client from functioning.

Proposed Changes

Disabling the feature

This feature can be disabled on the broker and the client.

For the broker, leave client.configs.plugin.class unset (the RPCs are not advertised), or set client.configs.requested.keys empty to stop collection without a roll (see Configuration -> Broker).

For the client, set enable.configs.push to false: the client does not send any of the 2 requests and behaves exactly like a client without the feature. 

Broker Behaviour

  • GetClientConfigsSubscription and PushClientConfigs are included in ApiVersionsResponse only when client.configs.plugin.class is set
    • a request for either RPC while the feature is off gets a response with UNSUPPORTED_VERSION
  • no authorization performed by the broker on any of the 2 RPCs
    • any authenticated client may ask what is requested and report its own configuration
    • the plugin receives the principal and may apply its own authorization rule
  • when receiving a GetClientConfigsSubscription request the broker checks that the request header carries a valid client instance id (KIP-1313, INVALID_REQUEST otherwise) and returns the current value of the config client.configs.requested.keys. The plugin is not invoked.
  • when receiving a PushClientConfigs request the broker performs the following steps in this order:
    • validate push
      • checks the snapshot size against client.configs.max.bytes (CLIENT_CONFIGS_TOO_LARGE)
      • checks that it's well-formed (e.g., including the ClientType)
      • checks that the request header carries a valid client instance id (KIP-1313), otherwise INVALID_REQUEST
    • filter configs against the requested set
      • entries not named in the current requested set, and entries typed UNKNOWN (keys the sending client does not define), are dropped before the plugin and logged at DEBUG by key name.
      • this makes the operator's setting hold for every client library (considering clients that may not filter) 
      • the plugin is invoked even if nothing remains, with an empty ClientConfigs
    • invoke plugin (returns a future)
    • respond with ErrorCode=NONE without waiting for the plugin's future
      • the future's outcome, including a synchronous throw, is recorded in the broker's metrics and logs and is not reported to the client
  • no storage or persisted state in the broker. Every accepted snapshot is handed to the plugin and then forgotten; a resend reaches the plugin again
    • with this, the broker cannot tell apart a client that is older than this KIP or has enable.configs.push=false (sends neither request), a client whose push was rejected as too large, and a client that gave up after no response. Every client that implements KIP-1313 sends its client instance id, so a system that records instance ids can still list the instances that never pushed.

Configuration payload size enforcement

Clients only send the requested keys that belong to them, so a snapshot is small. As a backup, the broker checks the snapshot size of every PushClientConfigs request against client.configs.max.bytes before invoking the plugin. If the snapshot is larger, the broker answers CLIENT_CONFIGS_TOO_LARGE, with the limit in the error message, and nothing reaches the plugin.

A client's share of the default requested set is a few hundred bytes. The limit only matters if an operator requests every key a client defines. The table shows that worst case for the Java clients, so a default of 10 KB leaves room:


Client

A default 10 KB limit provides 2x headroom for a Kafka Streams snapshot with every key requested, and more than 10x for the default requested set, while preventing abuse from malicious clients.

Excluding sensitive configurations

  • sensitive configs are filtered out by every client before any value is rendered (hardcoded sensitive set)
  • the broker does not check sensitivity
  • the broker only drops entries that are not in the requested set and entries typed UNKNOWN (see above)
  • a plugin may drop more (for example class-name keys); the client is not told about it

Metrics

The following broker metrics are added, in the group client-configs:

Client Behaviour

Exchange

The exchange runs on the client's own network thread (producer sender thread, consumer and share consumer background thread, admin client thread; for the classic consumer its network polling logic). It never blocks a user API call.

  1. the exchange starts when enable.configs.push  is true on the client and a connection's ApiVersionsResponse advertises both RPCs
  2. the client sends GetClientConfigsSubscription to the least-loaded connected node that supports both RPCs
    1. If RequestedConfigs in the response is empty, the client logs one DEBUG line and the exchange is complete.
    2. otherwise the client builds the snapshot from the keys that pass the filtering (possibly none, see Configurations sent) and sends one PushClientConfigs per snapshot (its own, and a framework's if one is registered, see Client API).
      1. when it sends the push it logs one INFO line naming the keys it pushes and the requested keys it filtered out, with the reason (sensitive/denied/not defined), never the values. With this an application can audit from its own log what left the process
      2. each push ends at its first response, success or error
      3. the exchange is complete when every push has ended
    3. if a request gets no response (e.g., disconnect, request timeout):
      1. the client retries it after retry.backoff.ms, growing up to retry.backoff.max.ms
      2. then continues retrying with backoff until default.api.timeout.ms elapses (config available for consumer, share consumer and admin but not producer). Producer retries capped at 3 attempts
      3. each retry goes to the least-loaded node that advertises both RPCs, preferring a node other than the one that did not respond. It goes back to the same node only when no other node advertising both RPCs is available
      4. if no success after all retries the client logs the failure at WARN and the exchange is complete
  3. the exchange is independent of the KIP-714 telemetry RPCs (GetTelemetrySubscriptions, PushTelemetry): there is no ordering between them, they may run at the same time, and they may go to different brokers
  4. the client only sends to a node that advertises both RPCs. If none of the known brokers advertise the RPCs, the client sends nothing and re-evaluates at each new connection (based on the ApiVersionsResponse).
  5. the exchange runs once per client instance (plus one more for a framework snapshot registered after it completed, see Client API)
    1. reconnects do not run it again
    2. later changes to the requested set are seen only by clients that run their exchange after it
  6. when a client is closed there is no specific action related to configs (it just drops pending config requests if there is any)

Kafka Streams

A Kafka Streams application reports its own configuration via its admin client, in addition to what its embedded clients report.

  • KafkaStreams calls registerLogicalClientConfigs on its admin client (one per instance), passing its framework name (KIP-1368) and its StreamsConfig
  • the admin client runs one exchange, or a second one for the Streams snapshot alone if its own exchange completed before the registration (see Client API)
    • when keys are requested, it pushes its own snapshot with ClientType=admin, and the Streams snapshot (StreamsConfig) with ClientType set to the framework name
  • all snapshots of one Streams instance (embedded producers, consumers, admin client, and the Streams snapshot) arrive on connections that carry the same framework id (KIP-1368), so a plugin can group them
  • enable.configs.push defined in a KafkaStreams application follows the usual Streams rules for client configs:
    • the value in StreamsConfig applies to every embedded client
    • a value prefixed for one client (for example admin.enable.configs.push) applies to that client only (overwrites the unprefixed one)
    • because the admin default is false, Kafka Streams sets enable.configs.push=true on its admin client unless the application sets it
    • if the application sets admin.enable.configs.push=false, the admin client sends neither request, so the Streams snapshot is not pushed

Kafka Connect

  • this KIP adds no Connect-level snapshot
  • worker and connector configuration is a separate surface (KIP-458 already governs which client configurations a connector may override) and is out of scope of this KIP
  • the workers' embedded clients answer the requested set like any client
    • they carry the framework name and version from KIP-1368 (and, for clients that serve a connector, its framework id), so a plugin can group or drop them

Compatibility, Deprecation, and Migration Plan

Impact on existing applications

These are the combinations of client and broker ("old" means before this KIP so not supporting config observability, "new" means post-KIP). For new brokers it also distinguishes whether a plugin is configured and whether any keys are requested, since those decide what happens.

ClientBrokerBehaviour
New, enable.configs.push=trueNew, plugin configured, keys requested
  • RPCs advertised
  • the client gets the requested configs and pushes them
  • plugin invoked
New, enable.configs.push=trueNew, plugin configured, nothing requested
  • RPCs advertised
  • the client gets the requested configs, sends nothing
  • plugin not invoked
NewNew without a plugin or Old (pre-KIP)
  • RPCs not advertised
  • the client sends nothing
OldNew
  • RPCs advertised when a plugin is configured, but an old client does not know them and sends nothing
  • plugin (if any) not invoked
New, enable.configs.push=falseAny
  • same as an old client
  • the client sends neither request, whatever the broker advertises
  • plugin not invoked.

Migration

This is a purely additive feature and requires no migration.

  • Before: no client configuration visibility
  • After: incremental visibility as clients upgrade

Test Plan

The feature will be covered by unit, integration and system tests, with a test-only logging plugin where needed. They verify that:

  • sensitive configurations never leave the client, whatever the cluster requests
  • each client type, Kafka Streams included, pushes only the requested keys it defines, checked against the default requested set
  • the exchange never blocks or fails a user API call, including when a broker does not respond
  • the broker drops what it did not request and keeps plugin failures away from clients
  • clients behave correctly in mixed-version clusters and when the feature is enabled on a running cluster

Rejected Alternatives

  1. A client-owned key set: per-client default lists, application override through config.push.allowed.keys, and a single PushConfig request with no way for the cluster to ask for anything. Rejected as this approach makes broker-side observability very limited, where the ultimate goal is to provide observability to broker/operator.
  2. A blocking handshake before the first user request. Rejected as it adds latency to the first request for no correctness gain (the broker learns nothing that it can act on sooner).
  3. A synchronous ClientConfigPolicy extending Reconfigurable, with a "process(...)" invoked on the request-handler thread. Rejected as "policy" implies validation the interface does not perform, also a synchronous call holds a request-handler thread for the plugin's latency. Rejected in favour of an asynchronous ClientConfigsPlugin approach, similar to KIP-1331.
  4. A broker-side sensitivity check: Rejected as the broker cannot judge key names across client libraries, and the client could not act on a violation since this KIP has no rejection semantics. Sensitive configs are filtered out by every client before any value is rendered.
  5. client_instance_id broker metrics and an instance-count gauge, were initially proposed in the KIP. Per-instance tags would bring unbounded cardinality, and the broker keeps no per-instance state to expire them with. Also an instance count has no clear value for an exchange that runs once per client instance. Both rejected.
  6. Omitting entries that hold their default value. Rejected because the push happens once per client lifetime and is a few kilobytes, so the saving is negligible. A plugin can drop default-valued entries itself.
  7. Never sending class-name keys (key.serializer, partitioner.class, interceptor.classes and similar). Considered initially, but they seems valuable, as they are a frequent root cause in client support cases. Also they only reveal package naming and the choice of serializers/interceptors/partitioners, but not credentials, endpoints or data. They are not in the default requested set, and an application can deny them.
  8. A ClientInstanceId field added to ApiVersionsRequest, considered in the first draft of this KIP. Not needed after KIP-1313.
  9. Others from the discussion thread on the initial KIP design:
    1. Sending the configurations as KIP-714 client metrics. Rejected because a configuration is a one-time snapshot of named values (many of them strings, lists or class names), while KIP-714 pushes numeric time series periodically on a subscription. Replaced by the two dedicated RPCs of this KIP.
    2. Sending every value as a plain string with no type. Favouring a type that lets a plugin interpret values without knowing each client library's configuration definitions. The type reuses the existing ConfigEntry.ConfigType, so there is no new enum to map.
    3. Sending custom configurations (keys the client does not define) when the cluster requests them. Left out of scope. A later KIP can add them with an explicit opt-in from the application.
    4. Giving a framework such as Kafka Streams its own client instance id and pushing its snapshot under it. Rejected because a framework has no connection of its own. Replaced by pushing the snapshot through one of its clients with ClientType set to the framework name. The KIP-1368 framework id groups it with the framework's other clients.
    5. Returning the requested keys in ApiVersionsResponse. Rejected because ApiVersions runs on every connection, while the list is needed once per client instance.
    6. Returning the requested keys in the push response. We did assess the push-response option as a single RPC serving both purposes (a push with no entries to ask, then a push with the values), but it seemed more confusing: two RPCs hidden in one relying on null/empty mode, with unused fields in each mode and one shared version range, error table and set of per-API metrics. KIP-714 splits exactly these two steps, so this KIP follows that shape at the cost of one more apiKey.

results.title: KIP-1325: Add restore.buffered.records.per.partition to cap Kafka Streams state-restore memory

storage.value:
Status

Current state: Accepted

Discussion thread: here 

Vote thread: here

JIRA: here 

Motivation

Kafka Streams allows users to configure many different memory limits, to pro-actively manage memory usage to avoid OutOfMemory errors.

However, on the restore code path, there is no such memory management. The `StoreChangelogReader` fetches a batch of messages, and buffers them inside `ChangelogMetadata`, and there is no limit enforced on this buffer, eventually leading to OutOfMemoryError during backfills. So only in the normal processing path, streams enforce a buffer limit via buffered.records.per.partition (default 1000), but when restore happens, there is no such logic in StoreChangelogReader. A brief discussion here as well.

This kip introduces a config in StreamsConfig 'restore.buffered.records.per.partition' to cap the per-partition restore buffer.


Public Interfaces

1. New StreamsConfig configuration


java

There are no other public changes.

Proposed Changes

  • Register the new config

In `streams/src/main/java/org/apache/kafka/streams/StreamsConfig.java`, add the constant alongside the existing `BUFFERED_RECORDS_PER_PARTITION_CONFIG` block and register it in the `ConfigDef` :

java


  • Read the config in `StoreChangelogReader`

StoreChangelogReader already takes a `StreamsConfig` in its constructor. Read the new value once and store it as:

java

and initialized in the constructor from `config.getInt(StreamsConfig.RESTORE_BUFFERED_RECORDS_PER_PARTITION_CONFIG)`.


  • Enforce the buffer cap via pause / resume

`StoreChangelogReader` already pauses and resumes partitions on the restore consumer through `pauseResumePartitions(...)` and `updatePartitionsByType(...)`.

The new enforcement reuses the same mechanism with minor enhancement:

  • Before polling - shouldPause() method (`pollRecordsFromRestoreConsumer`): for every currently restoring partition whose `ChangelogMetadata.bufferedRecords.size() >= restoreMaxBufferedRecordsPerPartition`, add it to the pause set. This prevents the restore consumer from fetching more data for partitions whose buffer is already full.
  • After draining – shouldResume() method (`restoreChangelog`): once records have been applied to the state store and `bufferedRecords.size() < restoreMaxBufferedRecordsPerPartition`, the partition becomes eligible for resume on the next `pauseResumePartitions(...)` call.

This is just a filter on top of existing pause-resume functionality and both paths normal and restore (buffered.records.per.partition and restore.buffered.records.per.partition ) go through the same poll/buffer/restore loop.


  • introduce a lower bound to avoid bouncing between pause and resume

 For example, a paused partition should only be resumed once the buffered records drop below 50% of the max capacity. To decide this. benchmark the frequent switching between pause and resume. It can be a follow up.

  • Documentation
    • Add the new config to the "Streams Configs" reference at `docs/streams/developer-guide/config-streams.html`, adjacent to `buffered.records.per.partition`, with a clear note that the two configs target different code paths.
    • Add a short note in the upgrade guide for the target release, calling out the new default cap on restore-path buffering
    • Update the "Memory Management" section of the Streams developer guide to list restore-path buffering alongside cache.


Compatibility, Deprecation, and Migration Plan

Compatibility

For users who do not set the new config, unbounded buffering to buffering capped at 10000 recs per partition. For better throughput on restore, during large backfills, increase the config.

Deprecation - na-

Migration

No user action is required. Users concerned about a throughput regression can explicitly set `restore.buffered.records.per.partition` to a larger value (e.g., `100000`) to approximate the previous unbounded behavior for typical deployments.

Test Plan

Adds unit and integration test coverage and mainly trigger restoration, asserting restoration is finished successfully.

Rejected Alternatives

We can apply the same config buffered.records.per.partition in StoreChangelogReader, but 1000 looks low, as it can slow down restoration and we should also consider polling. If polling is faster and restore is slow, we notice a lag.

results.title: KIP-1327: Prevent Hot Data Loss on Partition Expansion for Reset Offset Policy

storage.value:
Status

Current state: Withdraw

Discussion thread: https://lists.apache.org/thread/bp4zk31zr1sdxjsspg7b7bqddmm9t4gn

Vote Thread: https://lists.apache.org/thread/dgs3t9xmmldof5mmhwp21rpl3mfvpfw1

JIRA: ASF JIRA5aa69414-a9e9-3523-82ec-879b028fb15bKAFKA-20539

Motivation

When a Kafka topic is expanded with new partitions, consumers configured with auto.offset.reset=latest will silently miss every record produced to those new partitions. This data loss occurs during the metadata blindness window, the gap between when the partition is created on the broker and when the consumer discovers it during its next periodic metadata refresh. No exception is thrown, no warning is emitted, and no log entry is generated.

Partition expansion is a routine operational procedure, not an exceptional event. Topics are typically created with a conservative partition count and scaled up as throughput grows; nearly every long-lived, high-volume topic will undergo expansion at some point in its lifecycle. Under the current behavior, each such expansion is a silent data-loss opportunity for auto.offset.reset=latest consumers — making data loss an expected outcome of a common operational workflow, not an edge case.

The root cause is that auto.offset.reset is applied uniformly to every partition without a committed offset, regardless of when that partition was created relative to the consumer group. From the user's perspective, however, two cases are fundamentally different:

  • Partitions that existed before the consumer group was created. The choice of auto.offset.reset reflects an informed decision about how to handle the historical backlog that predates the group. Selecting latest is an explicit acknowledgment that pre-group history will not be consumed.
  • Partitions added to the topic after the consumer group was created. Every record on such a partition was produced during the group's active lifetime. Skipping these records with latest is not an informed choice — it is silent data loss in a window where the user expects continuous, gap-free consumption.

Today there is no way to express different reset behavior for these two cases. None of latest, earliest, none, or by_duration allows scoping the policy to one category, and application-level workarounds such as custom ConsumerRebalanceListener.onPartitionsAssigned() logic lack the temporal metadata needed to distinguish them reliably.

This KIP introduces a complementary configuration, auto.offset.reset.new.partitions, that decouples the reset policy for partitions added after group creation from the policy for partitions that predate it. The new configuration accepts the same value space as auto.offset.reset (earliest, latest, by_duration:<duration>), enabling users to express their actual intent. For example, combining auto.offset.reset=latest with auto.offset.reset.new.partitions=earliest ensures that pre-group history is skipped while no record on a newly expanded partition is silently lost.

Classification is deterministic and server-side: the broker compares the group's creation timestamp (recorded once and propagated via ConsumerGroupHeartbeatResponse) against the partition's creation time. Partitions created after the group are classified as newly expanded. This eliminates fragile client-side heuristics relying on metadata refresh intervals.

Why Existing Alternatives are Insufficient

Custom ConsumerRebalanceListener.onPartitionsAssigned() logic

Clients currently have no way to determine when a partition was created, partition creation time is entirely absent from MetadataResponse, a protocol gap this KIP closes. Without that timestamp, user code must resort to heuristics such as treating any previously unseen partition ID as newly expanded. These heuristics break under ordinary operational conditions, consumer restarts, group migrations, partition reassignments, and topic re-subscriptions, surfacing pre-existing partitions as "new" and triggering exactly the kind of massive historical reprocessing we want to avoid. Preventing silent data loss on partition expansion is correctness-critical behavior and belongs in the core client, not reimplemented by every application.

by_duration

The existing by_duration policy may appear to address partition-expansion data loss, but has three limitations that make it unsuitable:

  1. The seek target is computed client-side as now() - duration, introducing clock skew across consumers and forcing operators to choose large durations at the cost of unnecessary reprocessing.
  2. The target timestamp is recomputed on each retry, so failed ListOffsetsRequest retries can shift the target forward, causing records produced between attempts to be missed.
  3. It applies uniformly to all partitions missing a committed offset, failing to distinguish genuinely new partitions from pre-existing ones newly assigned to the group, which forces unnecessary replay

auto.offset.reset.new.partitions combined with the group-creation-time classifier addresses all three. Classification is derived from two server-recorded timestamps partition.creationTime (set once at partition creation) and group.creationTime (set once at group creation), eliminating any dependency on the consumer's clock. Because both timestamps are fixed at creation and never updated, classification is deterministic and stable across retries. And because classification is per-partition, only genuinely new partitions are affected; pre-existing partitions newly assigned to the group continue to follow the base auto.offset.reset policy.

Even users who choose auto.offset.reset=by_duration as their base policy benefit from this decoupling: setting auto.offset.reset.new.partitions to an explicit value (e.g., earliest) confines the by_duration seek-back semantics to pre-existing partitions, where they are appropriate, while newly expanded partitions follow the dedicated new-partition policy.

Public Interfaces

New Consumer Configuration

auto.offset.reset.new.partitions

PropertyValue
TypeString 
Defaultnull
Valid Valuesearliest, latest, by_duration:<duration>

Specifies the offset reset policy to apply to newly expanded partitions (i.e., partitions whose creation on the broker postdates the consumer group's creation timestamp). When a partition has a committed offset that is out of the available range (e.g., due to log truncation), the consumer applies the base auto.offset.reset policy regardless of the partition's creation timestamp. This config only affects partitions with no committed offset at all.

  • If a partition has a committed offset, this configuration has no effect. The consumer resumes from the committed offset as usual.
  • If a partition has no committed offset, the consumer applies the reset policy selected by the group coordinator. The group coordinator classifies partitions server-side and reports the result through a per-topic side channel: ConsumerGroupHeartbeatResponse.Assignment.TopicPartitions[].NewPartitions is a tagged []int32 containing the subset of partition indices in Partitions that are classified as newly expanded.
    • Partition index ∈ NewPartitions → apply auto.offset.reset.new.partitions.
    • Partition index ∉ NewPartitions → apply the base auto.offset.reset.
  • When connected to a broker that does not support the new heartbeat version, NewPartitions is absent (and therefore defaults to an empty list). As a result, every partition is treated as pre-existing and the base auto.offset.reset is applied uniformly. The new behavior becomes effective automatically once the brokers are upgraded.

When this config is unset (default), the consumer applies the base auto.offset.reset uniformly to all partitions without committed offsets.

Interaction matrix

The full interaction between the base policy and the new-partition policy:

  2. Real-time consumer that wants bounded recovery on new partitions (e.g., last hour) without replaying years of history.
  3. Backfill on first deployment but treat post-deployment partition expansions as live-only.
  4. Time-windowed consumer that wants a different lookback for newly created partitions than for pre-existing ones

Kafka Streams

auto.offset.reset in Kafka Streams applies only to source topics and repartition topics. Changelog topics and global state topics always use none for offset reset and are restored independently by StoreChangelogReader and GlobalStreamThread, respectively. As a result, auto.offset.reset.new.partitions does not apply to those topics.

At the StreamsConfig level, users can configure auto.offset.reset.new.partitions to apply a reset policy for newly added partitions across all source topics in the application. It has the same value space, default value, and semantics as the consumer configuration of the same name.

For per-source-topic overrides, org.apache.kafka.streams.AutoOffsetReset gains a new method, withNewPartitionsResetPolicy(...), which attaches a new-partitions reset policy to an existing AutoOffsetReset instance. The existing precedence rules remain unchanged: if a source topic specifies a Consumed.withOffsetResetPolicy(...) override, that policy (including its attached new-partitions policy, if present) takes precedence. Otherwise, the topic uses the pair of global settings configured through StreamsConfig.

Example:

Share groups

share.auto.offset.reset.new.partitions

PropertyValue
TypeString 
Defaultnull
Valid Valuesearliest, latest, by_duration:<duration>

A group-level dynamic configuration that parallels the existing share.auto.offset.reset. Like its base counterpart, it is configured on a share group and is consumed by the broker when the share-partition coordinator initializes a partition's Share Partition Start Offset (SPSO).

Its semantics mirror those of auto.offset.reset.new.partitions for consumer groups and Kafka Streams:

  • If the SPSO has already been persisted for a (group, topic, partition), this configuration has no effect.

  • If the SPSO has not yet been persisted, the share-partition coordinator classifies the partition server-side using the same algorithm:

    partition.creationTime > group.creationTime

    The classification result is propagated to the partition leader through the share-state persister path (see Schema Changes).

    • Classified as newly expanded → initialize the SPSO using share.auto.offset.reset.new.partitions.
    • Classified as pre-existing → initialize the SPSO using the base share.auto.offset.reset.
  • If share.auto.offset.reset.new.partitions is not configured (the default), the coordinator ignores the classification result and initializes the SPSO using the base share.auto.offset.reset for all partitions. This differs from the current behavior.

The interaction matrix has the same shape as the consumer configuration described above, except that "seek to LEO" becomes "initialize the SPSO to the LEO on first fetch", and "seek to offset 0" becomes "initialize the SPSO to the log start offset". Because share consumers do not support the none policy, the corresponding row does not apply.

Note: The StreamsGroupHeartbeat RPC version (v2) assumes that KIP-1331's version bump (v0 → v1) has been merged first. If the merge order changes, the version numbers will be adjusted accordingly during implementation.

InitializeShareGroupStateRequest — Adds a tagged IsNewPartition (bool) field (tag 0) to each PartitionData. Carries the share-group coordinator's partition classification to the share-state persister when a share-partition is first initialized.

group.creationTime) at the moment the share-partition state was initialized. The share-coordinator persists this value alongside the snapshot so the partition leader can apply share.auto.offset.reset.new.partitions when computing the SPSO. False (and absent) on older coordinators." } ]} ]} ] }]]>

ReadShareGroupStateResponse — Adds a tagged IsNewPartition (bool) field (tag 0) to each PartitionResult. Returns the persisted partition classification to the partition leader when SharePartition.maybeInitialize() reads the share state.


Record Schemas

PartitionRecord — Adds tagged field CreationTimeMs at tag 3. The controller persists this value once when the partition is initially created; it is never updated thereafter. Because the field is tagged, no schema version bump is required: existing brokers silently ignore the unknown tag, while upgraded brokers populate it for all newly created partitions going forward.

ConsumerGroupMetadataValue — Adds tagged field CreationTimeMs at tag 0, recorded once when the share group is first created.

StreamsGroupMetadataValue — Adds tagged field CreationTimeMs at tag 1, recorded once when the consumer group is first created.

ShareGroupMetadataValue — Adds tagged field CreationTimeMs at tag 1, recorded once when the consumer group is first created.

ShareSnapshotValue — Adds a tagged IsNewPartition (bool) field (tag 1). Persists the partition classification in the initial snapshot so that it survives broker and share-state persister restarts. The persisted value is returned in every subsequent ReadShareGroupStateResponse.


Feature Gating (MetadataVersion)

PartitionRecord is persisted in the KRaft metadata log. Every broker in the cluster reads from the same log and must agree on which tagged fields the controller is allowed to emit. To ensure this, this KIP introduces a new MetadataVersion:

  • Name: IBP_4_4_IV1
  • Description: Add PartitionRecord.CreationTimeMs tagged field (KIP-1327).
  • Accessor: MetadataVersion.isPartitionCreationTimeSupported() (returns true for IBP_4_4_IV1 and later).

Before the cluster's active MetadataVersion reaches IBP_4_4_IV1, the controller does not write CreationTimeMs, even when running a broker binary that supports the feature. Once the cluster is upgraded to IBP_4_4_IV1, every newly created PartitionRecord includes the field.

Feature Gating (GroupVersion / StreamsVersion / ShareVersion)

Wire compatibility is provided by the new RPC versions together with the tagged CreationTimeMs and IsNewPartition fields. Older clients ignore unknown response fields, while newer clients automatically fall back when communicating with coordinators that do not support the updated protocol versions.

Coordinator behavior, however, must also be gated. Whether a coordinator records CreationTimeMs when a group is created and whether it computes and emits NewPartitions or IsNewPartition must be consistent across all coordinator replicas. Otherwise, during a rolling upgrade, leadership could move between upgraded and not-yet-upgraded brokers, causing CreationTimeMs to be recorded inconsistently or classification results to appear in some responses but not others.

To ensure consistent behavior, this KIP introduces a new feature level for each of the existing feature tracks, following the same feature-gating pattern used by GV_1, StreamsVersion.SV_1, and ShareVersion.SV_1.

GroupVersion

GroupVersion gates the consumer-group coordinator only.

  • Name: GV_2
  • Description: Enable partition-expansion classification for consumer groups (KIP-1327).
  • Accessor: GroupVersion.isNewPartitionsClassificationSupported() (returns true for GV_2 and later).
  • Dependency: metadata.version = IBP_4_4_IV1, so partition.creationTime is available in the metadata image.

Before the cluster's active group.version reaches GV_2, the consumer-group coordinator neither records ConsumerGroupMetadataValue.CreationTimeMs when creating a consumer group nor computes or emits NewPartitions in ConsumerGroupHeartbeatResponse, even when running on a broker binary that supports the feature.

Once the cluster reaches GV_2, both behaviors become active for consumer groups created after the upgrade.

StreamsVersion

StreamsVersion gates the streams-group coordinator only.

  • Name: SV_2
  • Description: Enable partition-expansion classification for Streams groups (KIP-1327).
  • Accessor: StreamsVersion.isNewPartitionsClassificationSupported() (returns true for SV_2 and later).
  • Dependency: metadata.version = IBP_4_4_IV1.

SV_2 has the same semantics as GV_2, but applies to the streams-group coordinator. It gates recording StreamsGroupMetadataValue.CreationTimeMs when creating a Streams group and emitting NewPartitions in StreamsGroupHeartbeatResponse.

ShareVersion

ShareVersion gates the share-group coordinator only. Since ShareVersion.SV_2 is already reserved by KIP-1191 for the share-group DLQ feature, this KIP introduces SV_3.

  • Name: SV_3
  • Description: Enable partition-expansion classification for share groups (KIP-1327).
  • Accessor: ShareVersion.isNewPartitionsClassificationSupported() (returns true for SV_3 and later).
  • Dependency: metadata.version = IBP_4_4_IV1.

ShareVersion.SV_1 is already a transitive prerequisite because share groups themselves must be enabled before any per-share-group behavior is meaningful, so no additional dependency is required.

Before the cluster's active share.version reaches SV_3, the share-group coordinator neither records ShareGroupMetadataValue.CreationTimeMs when creating a share group nor includes IsNewPartition in InitializeShareGroupStateRequest. Consequently, the persisted IsNewPartition value defaults to false, and SharePartition always applies the base share.auto.offset.reset, regardless of whether share.auto.offset.reset.new.partitions is configured.

Once the cluster reaches SV_3, these behaviors become active for share groups created after the upgrade and for share-partitions initialized after the upgrade.

Proposed Changes

Classification Algorithm

Classification is performed server-side by the group coordinator: the consumer-group coordinator for consumer groups, and the streams-group coordinator for Streams groups. In both cases, the coordinator computes a NewPartitions subset for each assignment—of Partitions for consumer groups and of each task's partition list for Streams groups—and includes it in the assignment. The client simply checks whether a partition index is present in NewPartitions and applies the corresponding reset policy.

Group coordinator

For each topic included in a heartbeat assignment, the group coordinator computes NewPartitions from the following inputs:

  • partition.creationTime — read from the metadata image (PartitionRecord.CreationTimeMs), which is already replicated to both the consumer-group coordinator and the streams-group coordinator.
  • group.creationTime — read from the in-memory group state, populated from ConsumerGroupMetadataValue.CreationTimeMs or StreamsGroupMetadataValue.CreationTimeMs.

A partition is included in NewPartitions if: partition.creationTime > group.creationTime

If either timestamp is -1 (the upgrade fallback value), the comparison uses conservative defaults. An unknown group.creationTime is treated as -∞, so any partition with a known creation time is classified as new. An unknown partition.creationTime is treated as pre-existing the consumer group. The following table summarizes all possible combinations:


group.creationTimepartition.creationTimeIn `NewPartitions`?Configuration applied
(when auto.offset.reset.new.partitions is set)
knownknown, > groupyesauto.offset.reset.new.partitions 
knownknown, ≤ groupnoauto.offset.reset 
known-1noauto.offset.reset 
-1knownyesauto.offset.reset.new.partitions 
-1-1noauto.offset.reset 

Consumer

If auto.offset.reset.new.partitions is not configured, the consumer ignores NewPartitions and applies the base auto.offset.reset to every partition without a committed offset. This is the default behavior.

If auto.offset.reset.new.partitions is configured, then for each partition without a committed offset:

  • If the partition index is present in NewPartitions, apply auto.offset.reset.new.partitions.
  • Otherwise, apply the base auto.offset.reset.

Server-Side Timestamp Recording

Both CreationTimeMs fields are write-once on the server side. Once recorded, they are never overwritten — neither by subsequent metadata-log entries (for partitions) nor by group lifecycle events (for groups). This immutability is what makes classification deterministic and stable across retries.

PartitionRecord.CreationTimeMs

The controller writes a PartitionRecord exactly once per partition, at the moment of initial creation, whether via topic creation or CreatePartitionsRequest, and records CreationTimeMs from its current wall-clock time at that point.

All subsequent partition state changes (leader elections, ISR updates, replica reassignments, ELR / LastKnownElr updates, log-directory changes, etc.) are written as PartitionChangeRecord, a distinct metadata record type that does not carry CreationTimeMs. The original timestamp from the initial PartitionRecord is therefore never overwritten, and remains the authoritative value for the lifetime of the partition.

Partitions that existed before the broker upgrade have no CreationTimeMs in their original PartitionRecord (the tagged field is simply absent) and read as -1 (unknown) on the wire. Such partitions are always classified as pre-existing — the safer default, as it aligns with the user's intent when selecting the base auto.offset.reset.

ConsumerGroupMetadataValue.CreationTimeMs and StreamsGroupMetadataValue.CreationTimeMs

The group coordinator sets CreationTimeMs to its current wall-clock time when it writes the first metadata value for a group—that is, when a member sends the first ConsumerGroupHeartbeatRequest (consumer groups) or StreamsGroupHeartbeatRequest (Streams groups) and the group does not yet exist.

Subsequent writes (epoch bumps, member joins and leaves, rebalances, metadata-hash changes) preserve the original CreationTimeMs. If a group is deleted (via DeleteGroupsRequest or expiration) and later re-created, a new CreationTimeMs is recorded. As a result, all partitions assigned to the re-created group are classified relative to the new group lifetime. Existing partitions are therefore classified as pre-existing, which is the intended behavior because a re-created group represents a clean slate from the user's perspective.

Groups that existed before the upgrade have no CreationTimeMs field and therefore read as -1 (unknown). During classification, an unknown group.creationTime is conservatively treated as -∞, so any partition with a known partition.creationTime is classified as new, while partitions whose partition.creationTime is also unknown are classified as pre-existing. This behavior is identical for both consumer groups and Streams groups.

Share Groups

Share groups differ from consumer and Streams groups in two ways that make the consumer-side classification path inapplicable:

  1. Reset is broker-side, not client-side. share.auto.offset.reset is a group-level dynamic configuration, and the initial Share Partition Start Offset (SPSO) is computed by SharePartition.startOffsetDuringInitialization on the partition leader the first time the share-partition is fetched—not by the share consumer. There is no client-side auto.offset.reset logic on which to layer a new policy.
  2. The partition leader is not the share-group coordinator. Classification requires group.creationTime, which is maintained by the share-group coordinator. The partition leader, where the SPSO is initialized, is typically a different broker and has no direct access to the group's state.

The existing share-state persister path naturally solves both problems:

  • The share-group coordinator performs classification once, when it first determines that a share-partition must be initialized via InitializeShareGroupStateRequest.
  • The persister carries the resulting IsNewPartition flag alongside the existing initialization payload, persists it in the snapshot, and returns it in every subsequent ReadShareGroupStateResponse.
  • During SPSO initialization, the partition leader reads IsNewPartition and selects either share.auto.offset.reset.new.partitions or the base share.auto.offset.reset accordingly.

Share-group Coordinator: Classification

When the share-group coordinator determines that a share-partition requires initialization (see GroupMetadataManager.subscribedTopicsChangeMap and maybeCreateInitializeShareGroupStateRequest), it also computes IsNewPartition for each partition included in the resulting InitializeShareGroupStateRequest.

The inputs are identical to those used by the consumer-group coordinator:

  • partition.creationTime — read from the metadata image (PartitionRecord.CreationTimeMs).
  • group.creationTime — read from ShareGroupMetadataValue.CreationTimeMs.

The same conservative classification rules described in Group coordinator apply. An unknown group.creationTime is treated as -∞, so partitions with a known creation time are classified as new. An unknown partition.creationTime is treated as pre-existing.

IsNewPartition is computed once, when the share-partition is initialized, and is then persisted. It is not recomputed later. This is intentional because SPSO itself is a one-time decision: once SharePartition initializes the SPSO, it never recomputes it. Recomputing the classification later would therefore have no effect and would introduce unnecessary divergence if group.creationTime were ever to change (it does not; see Server-Side Timestamp Recording).

ShareGroupMetadataValue.CreationTimeMs

The share-group coordinator records CreationTimeMs using its current wall-clock time when it writes the first ShareGroupMetadataValue for a group—that is, when it processes the first ShareGroupHeartbeatRequest for a group that does not yet exist.

Subsequent writes (epoch bumps and metadata-hash changes) preserve the original timestamp, following the same semantics as ConsumerGroupMetadataValue.CreationTimeMs.

As with consumer groups, deleting and re-creating a share group records a new CreationTimeMs. Consequently, partitions that already exist when the group is re-created are classified as pre-existing, matching the intended clean-slate behavior.

Share groups created before the upgrade have no CreationTimeMs field and therefore read as -1 (unknown). During classification, an unknown group.creationTime is conservatively treated as -∞, so any partition with a known partition.creationTime is classified as new and automatically benefits from partition-expansion protection.

Persister Path: IsNewPartition Propagation

The IsNewPartition flag travels through the existing share-state persister path:

  1. InitializeShareGroupStateRequest (coordinator → persister). The share-group coordinator includes IsNewPartition for each PartitionData in the request.
  2. ShareSnapshotValue (persister → metadata log). The share coordinator persists IsNewPartition in the initial snapshot for the share-partition. The field is immutable and is not carried in subsequent ShareUpdateValue records.
  3. ReadShareGroupStateResponse (persister → partition leader). When SharePartition.maybeInitialize() loads the share state, the persisted IsNewPartition value is returned on every read. Since SPSO initialization occurs at most once per share-partition lifetime, only the first read is relevant in practice.

All three fields are tagged with ignorable: true, ensuring safe behavior during rolling upgrades:

  • share.version < SV_3. The share-group coordinator does not emit IsNewPartition, so SharePartition applies the base share.auto.offset.reset for all share-partitions, matching pre-KIP-1327 behavior.
  • Older share-coordinator persister. The persister ignores the unknown tagged field on InitializeShareGroupStateRequest, causing IsNewPartition to be stored as its default value (false). SharePartition therefore applies the base share.auto.offset.reset.
  • Older partition leader. The leader ignores the unknown tagged field on ReadShareGroupStateResponse and continues applying the base share.auto.offset.reset. No incompatibility is introduced during rollout.

Partition Leader: SPSO Initialization

SharePartition.startOffsetDuringInitialization (currently core/src/main/java/kafka/server/share/SharePartition.java:3151) takes one additional input from ReadShareGroupStateResponse: IsNewPartition.

The initialization logic becomes:

  1. If partitionDataStartOffset != UNINITIALIZED_START_OFFSET, use the persisted SPSO. (Unchanged.)
  2. Otherwise, select the reset policy:
    • If IsNewPartition == true and share.auto.offset.reset.new.partitions is configured for the group, use share.auto.offset.reset.new.partitions.
    • Otherwise, use the base share.auto.offset.reset.
  3. Resolve the selected policy to an offset through metadataProvider.offsetFor*Timestamp(...), exactly as today.

The existing ShareGroupConfigProvider.autoOffsetReset(groupId) is extended with an overload autoOffsetReset(groupId, isNewPartition) to resolve the appropriate configuration.
