Rejected Alternatives

Rejected Alternatives to the Whole KIP

Application-Level Synchronous Replication

Leave synchronous cross-cluster replication to be handled at the application level, where applications manage their own dual-write logic or use caching/buffering to replay data to destination clusters.

Why Rejected:

  • Adds significant complexity to application code
  • No standardized solution that fits all use cases
  • Difficult to guarantee consistency and exactly-once semantics
  • Each application team would need to reinvent the wheel
  • Error handling and retry logic becomes application responsibility
  • Broker-level solution provides better performance and reliability guarantees

Promote Stretch Clusters for Zero-RPO in DR Situations

Recommend the use of stretched Kafka clusters (single logical cluster spanning multiple data centers) instead of separate clusters with mirroring.

Why Rejected:

  • Single failure domain — no isolation from software, configuration, or operational incidents. A stretched cluster is one logical cluster: a bad broker upgrade, a corrupted KRaft metadata log, a misapplied ACL change, a bad config rollout, a cascading failure, an inter-DC network partition that splits the controller quorum, or a runaway tenant propagates to every data center simultaneously, with no independent failover target to fall back to. There is no separate KRaft controller quorum, no separate metadata log — nothing to insulate failures, and no way to canary an upgrade in one DC for a release cycle before rolling it to the other. DR with two separate logical clusters exists primarily to protect against exactly these classes of incidents, which are the dominant cause of data-platform outages in practice — well above raw hardware failure or full-DC loss. With separate clusters plus sync mirroring, operators get the best of both worlds: zero data loss on failover and genuine fault isolation between primary and DR.
  • Cross-DC RTT becomes both a per-produce cost and an operational ceiling. Stretched clusters place replicas in different DCs, so any topic with acks=all and min.insync.replicas requiring cross-DC quorum blocks every produce on cross-DC RTT — regardless of whether that topic actually needs cross-DC durability. The same constraint imposes a hard operational ceiling on daily cluster work: partition rebalances, admin-client metadata traversals across nodes, consumer-group coordinator interactions, and similar control-plane operations all incur cross-DC round-trips and become correspondingly slow or unstable. Sync mirroring surfaces WAN-scale latencies to producers as longer ack times on the opted-in topics rather than as cluster instability or as limits on cluster operations; it is opt-in per topic, and works across regions and providers.
  • Vendor reality. Because of these operational limitations, no managed Kafka service offers stretched clusters as a managed product — operators who want this topology run it self-hosted at their own risk. Even in the self-hosted positioning, stretched clusters are framed as an HA mitigation for unstable hardware within a single cluster, not as a DR architecture. The operational requirements — dedicated low-latency interconnect, controller-quorum placement across DCs, ISR-aware client routing, careful tenant isolation — make them difficult to operate at scale, and the recovery semantics fundamentally do not match what operators expect from a DR setup.

Rejected Alternatives to Part of the KIP Decisions

Source Polling Destination for ISR Status

Instead of extending the FetchRequest to include remote replica information, have the source cluster actively poll the destination cluster to check if it has reached ISR for a given offset before acknowledging the producer.

Why Rejected:

  • Introduces a new request/response pattern instead of leveraging existing Kafka protocols
  • Less efficient than piggybacking on existing FetchRequest that already flows from destination to source
  • The existing producer acknowledgment mechanism already delays acks until all ISR replicas fetch the required offset; extending this to include remote replicas is a natural fit
  • In KIP-1279, the leader on the destination is already treated as a replica from the source's perspective, so extending the existing replication path is clearer and more consistent
  • Polling would add unnecessary network overhead and complexity
  • Harder to reason about timing and consistency with an additional RPC pattern

Sync/Async Selection in Producer Client API 

Allow producers to specify on a per-message basis whether to use synchronous or asynchronous mirroring (via configs or headers).

Why Rejected:

  • Would require significant changes to the producer API and force producers to upgrade their clients to achieve this functionality
  • If configuration is not consistent across all topic producers, it could lead to confusing behavior where some messages in a partition have different guarantees
  • Topic-level configuration is simpler and sufficient for most use cases

Automatic Degradation to Async Mode

Automatically downgrade from sync to async mode when destination cluster latency exceeds a threshold, without manual intervention.

Why Rejected:

  • Silent degradation could violate zero-RPO guarantees without operator awareness
  • May cause unexpected data loss in disaster scenarios. Operators should make explicit decisions about when to accept data loss risk
  • Difficult to determine appropriate thresholds that work for all use cases
  • Manual control provides clearer operational semantics
  • However this can be a follow-up improvement later to this KIP

Replica Fetch with Synthetic Replica ID for Sync Mirror

Use FetchRequest.forReplica with a synthetic negative replica ID (e.g., -3) for sync mirror fetches, so the source cluster treats the destination as a follower replica and returns data up to LEO.

Why Rejected:

  • The synthetic replica ID would create a fake entry in the source's remoteReplicasMap, which could confuse ISR shrink/expand logic, partition reassignment, and leader election
  • Multiple destination brokers fetching with the same synthetic ID (or different synthetic IDs) adds complexity to the source's replica tracking
  • Risk of unintended side effects in metrics, monitoring, and operational tooling that assumes replica IDs correspond to actual brokers
  • The source would need special-case handling in followerReplicaOrThrow and other validation paths to accept the synthetic ID
  • Cleaner alternative: use consumer-style fetch (replicaId=-1) and modify the source's read path to return data up to LEO when MirrorReplicaInfo is present in the FetchRequest. This keeps mirror fetches clearly separated from real replica fetches while still allowing the destination to catch up to LEO. The MirrorReplicaInfo becomes the single mechanism for both data flow (read up to LEO) and HW gating (destination ISR state), avoiding any pollution of the source's replica tracking

Mirror-Level ULE Pause Policy

Introduce a mirror-level configuration (e.g., mirror.sync.unclean.leader.election.policy with values PAUSE and FOLLOW) that controls what happens on the destination when the source experiences an unclean leader election. The PAUSE value (intended as default) would have the destination retain its authoritative data (potentially ahead of the new source leader), pause sync mirroring, and require the operator to decide between failing over, demoting to ASYNC, or releasing the sync link. The FOLLOW value would silently truncate to match the new source leader.

Why Rejected:

  • Re-invents the existing source-side unclean.leader.election.enable=false knob, which already prevents the data loss by blocking the unclean election entirely. Operators already have this primitive available without adding a new config surface
  • The PAUSE option's recovery path (operator chooses between failover-to-destination, demote-to-ASYNC, or source-side release) is already achievable today: blocking the unclean election on the source makes the partition unavailable, sync gating naturally pauses, and the operator can failover to the destination as new primary and later reverse-mirror to fail back (see the Unclean Leader Election on Source Cluster section above)
  • PAUSE-state semantics add substantial spec surface for a rare edge case: a new partition sub-state, paused-partition metric, operator decision tree, interaction with the source-side release flow, and recovery RPCs
  • Mirror-level naming would risk colliding with KIP-1279's existing mirror.support.unclean.leader.election topic config (which controls LME-truncation behavior on the destination), creating two configs with similar names but different semantics on the same resource
  • For V1, deferring this keeps sync and async modes consistent on source-ULE handling and limits the operational decision tree to existing Kafka primitives
  • This can be revisited in a follow-up KIP if the community demands explicit mirror-level handling beyond what the existing source-side unclean.leader.election.enable=false provides

Unify Register/Unregister into a Single RPC

A single MirrorSyncRegistrationOpRequest with an Operation enum (REGISTER/UNREGISTER) could replace the separate RegisterMirrorSyncTopicRequest and UnregisterMirrorSyncTopicRequest, saving one apiKey.

Why Rejected:

  • Separate RPCs make operation intent explicit at the protocol level — audit logs and wire traces show what was attempted without parsing an Operation discriminator
  • Register carries fields specific to admission control (RecoveryPromotion) that are meaningless on Unregister; merging them would make the unified schema harder to reason about
  • The apiKey conservation argument is minor; the protocol-key space is not constrained for mirror-related RPCs
  • Separate RPCs allow independent schema evolution in the future

Operator-Driven Recovery from Source-Side Release

Require an explicit operator action on the destination (--alter --sync after a release) to clear a destination-local "released-by-source" suppression flag and trigger re-promotion, rather than letting the destination's auto-promoter retry recovery automatically once lag reaches zero.

Why Rejected:

  • The two cases for source-side release have natural division of responsibility: destination unreachable from source is the only case --release-sync is for (the source operator is the only operator who can act); destination reachable but slow is handled by the destination operator running --alter --async. Once a destination becomes reachable again, the original justification for the source-side release no longer applies, and there is no operator intent to keep sync off
  • Operator-driven recovery would require a destination-side operator to manually clear suppression after every transient unreachability event — adding toil for a case the system can resolve on its own
  • The marker's defensive purpose (rejecting stale in-flight Registers from before release) is preserved either way: a stale Register carries RecoveryPromotion=false and is rejected; only a fresh recovery Register issued by the destination's auto-promoter (which the destination only fires after observing lag-zero) carries RecoveryPromotion=true and clears the marker
  • A destination operator who explicitly doesn't want auto-recovery can opt out by demoting the topic via --alter --async, which is the same primitive used for the reachable-but-slow case

results.title: KIP-1361 Change the default `auto.offset.reset` to `by_duration:PT5S`

storage.value:
Status

Current state: Under Discussion

Discussion thread: https://lists.apache.org/thread/njjznyly38td4scb9bjc8v0gq7kc1yqj

JIRA: here [Change the link from KAFKA-1 to your own ticket]

Motivation

The long-standing problem: silent data loss on partition expansion

Increasing a topic's partition count is a routine operational task, not an exceptional event. Topics are often created with a moderate number of partitions to balance cost and resource utilization, then expanded as workloads grow.

When a topic is expanded, a consumer configured with auto.offset.reset=latest can silently miss every record produced to the newly added partitions before the consumer becomes aware of them. The sequence is straightforward:

  • The topic is expanded, and the new partitions immediately begin receiving records.
  • The consumer does not learn about the new partitions until its next metadata refresh or assignment update. This creates a short metadata-blindness window.
  • When the consumer is assigned the new partitions, no committed offsets exist for them. As a result, auto.offset.reset applies. Under latest, the consumer seeks to the log end offset and skips all records produced during the blindness window.

The loss is completely silent: the consumer never observes the skipped records, and no error, warning, or metric indicates that data was lost. This remains one of the most common surprises associated with the latest reset policy.

Why previous proposals stalled

Two earlier KIPs attempted to address this issue by introducing new protocol-level mechanisms. Both ultimately became difficult to move forward because of their semantic and operational complexity.

KIP-1282 proposed a new reset policy, to_start_time, which anchors resets to the consumer group's creation timestamp. While this is an elegant fit for partition expansion, the proposal did not reach consensus on offset-out-of-range behavior. Under that design, a consumer whose committed offset is out of range would reset to earliest, while a consumer whose group metadata had been garbage-collected would reset to latest. Reviewers considered this behavior difficult to reason about and inconsistent with the principle that backlog should be treated uniformly.

KIP-1327 proposed an auxiliary configuration, auto.offset.reset.new.partitions, together with a group-creation-time-based classifier that distinguishes newly added partitions from existing ones. Implementing this requires persisting group creation timestamps, modifying on-disk record formats such as ConsumerGroupMetadataValue and PartitionRecord, adding new metadata-version and group-version gates, and extending GroupHeartbeatResponse with a NewPartitions field. The proposal also raised follow-on questions around share groups and mirrored clusters.

Taken together, these changes introduce substantial protocol and operational complexity to address what is usually a very small timing window.

Late in the KIP-1327 discussion, reviewers converged on a simpler observation: a by_duration value in the 5–10 second range already covers the common partition-expansion case, given the default heartbeat.interval.ms of 3 seconds. The residual reprocessing introduced by such a policy is also of the same order of magnitude as the small backlog that latest already tolerates between fetching the end offset and beginning consumption.

This KIP adopts that approach.

The key insight: a small replay window is safer than silent data loss

For an actively running consumer, the interval between partition creation and consumer discovery is bounded by the heartbeat and assignment cadence of the group protocol. Under default settings, this interval is typically only a few seconds: 5 seconds for the modern consumer group's group.consumer.heartbeat.interval.ms, and 3 seconds for the legacy heartbeat.interval.ms. This is the only period during which silent loss can occur for an actively running consumer.

KIP-1106 already provides a mechanism that naturally covers this window: by_duration. The policy resolves a reset position using a timestamp-based ListOffsets lookup at now() - duration.

For a partition created only seconds earlier, no records exist before that timestamp, so the lookup naturally resolves to the beginning of the partition and no records are lost. For a pre-existing partition assigned to a consumer without a committed offset, only the most recent few seconds of records are replayed.

This makes a small-duration default both practical and safe:

  • latest already tolerates a small amount of backlog. The latest policy is not a perfect zero-backlog policy. It inherently allows a small amount of backlog to accumulate between fetching the end offset and actually beginning consumption. Records produced during that gap are consumed after the reset. A bounded five-second replay window is of the same order of magnitude.
  • The safer failure mode is bounded replay. With latest, records can be silently and permanently skipped. With by_duration:PT5S, the worst-case outcome is a bounded re-read of a few seconds of recent data. Re-reading a small amount of recent data is generally harmless and self-correcting; silently skipping live data is not.

Why this proposal does not attempt to solve extended downtime

A recurring question in earlier discussions was how reset semantics should behave when a consumer is offline for an extended period while partitions are added.

This proposal does not attempt to special-case that scenario. Losing records produced to newly added partitions during an extended downtime is consistent with the semantics of latest. If a consumer is offline for a long period and a new partition is created during that downtime, a user who selected latest typically expects the consumer to resume from the current tail, not from the beginning of the new partition solely because the partition is technically new to the group.

A user who selects latest has already accepted that backlog accumulated during downtime may be skipped on any partition. Newly added partitions are not fundamentally different from existing partitions in this respect.

Attempting to distinguish "briefly unaware of a partition" from "offline for a week" introduces timing-dependent behavior that is difficult to explain and reason about. It also reintroduces the same protocol complexity that KIP-1282 and KIP-1327 attempted to manage.

by_duration:PT5S provides a clear and consistent boundary. It protects consumers from the short blindness window during which they had no opportunity to observe newly added partitions, while preserving the user's intent to ignore older backlog.

The "backlog is backlog" principle

The central observation is that historical data and live data differ only in the amount of backlog involved. Rather than introducing new reset policies or partition classifiers, users should have a single, consistent way to express how much backlog they are willing to tolerate when a reset occurs.

by_duration already provides that abstraction.

Changing the default from latest to a small non-zero duration transforms one of Kafka's most surprising default behaviors — silently losing live data after partition expansion — into a predictable and bounded behavior: replaying at most a few seconds of recent records. This achieves the desired outcome without introducing any new public APIs, RPCs, metadata records, or version-gated protocol changes.

Goals

  • Eliminate silent data loss during partition expansion for the common case of actively running consumers using the modern consumer group protocol.
  • Apply the same safe default consistently to the modern consumer and the share consumer. Kafka Streams is out of scope for this change because it already overrides the source-consumer reset policy to earliest through StreamsConfig.CONSUMER_DEFAULT_OVERRIDES.

Non-goals

  • This KIP does not attempt to change behavior for consumers that remain offline long enough to accumulate substantial backlog. Skipping such backlog is consistent with the intended semantics of latest.
  • This KIP does not change any Kafka Streams defaults. Streams already overrides auto.offset.reset to "earliest" for source and repartition consumers through StreamsConfig.CONSUMER_DEFAULT_OVERRIDES, and forces "none" for restore and global consumers. None of those paths are affected by this proposal.
  • This KIP does not tune behavior for the classic consumer protocol. The classic protocol is being removed in Kafka 5.0 under KIP-1274, and this proposal is targeted at the modern consumer group protocol and share groups.

Public Interfaces

This KIP introduces no new RPCs, metadata records, version gates, command-line flags, or configuration syntax. It changes only the default value of two existing reset-policy configurations.

ConfigurationOwnerOld defaultNew default
auto.offset.resetConsumerConfig (modern consumer)latestby_duration:PT5S
share.auto.offset.resetGroupConfig (share group, group-level)latestby_duration:PT5S

by_duration:PT5S is already a valid value for both configurations. This KIP changes only the default. 

The configuration documentation for both settings will be updated to describe the new default and explain the rationale for choosing a small non-zero duration.

Kafka Streams is not affected by this public-interface change. Streams applies its own reset-policy overrides on top of ConsumerConfig: source and repartition consumers default to "earliest", while restore and global consumers use "none". As a result, changing the ConsumerConfig default does not change any Streams-facing behavior.

Proposed Changes

Modern consumer

In ConsumerConfig, the default value supplied to the ConfigDef for AUTO_OFFSET_RESET_CONFIG is changed from "latest" to "by_duration:PT5S".

Under the new default, the reset position is resolved by issuing a timestamp-based ListOffsets lookup for now() - 5 seconds. For newly created partitions, this typically resolves to the beginning of the partition because no records exist before that timestamp. For existing partitions, it replays only a small, bounded amount of recent data.

Users who want the previous behavior can continue to set auto.offset.reset=latest explicitly.

Share consumer

Share groups have a different exposure surface from regular consumer groups.

Per KIP-932, share.auto.offset.reset applies when a share group first begins consuming an existing topic. In that case, the initial Share-Partition Start Offset (SPSO) for each partition is derived from share.auto.offset.reset.

However, when a topic that is already being consumed by a share group is expanded, the SPSO for each newly created share-partition is initialized to 0 by design. In that path, share.auto.offset.reset does not apply. This KIP does not change that behavior.

Therefore, changing the share-consumer default is not motivated by partition expansion, which is already safe for share groups. The motivation is consistency: users should not have to reason about a different default reset policy depending on which consumer type they use. A share group that starts consuming a busy existing topic should also avoid skipping all existing backlog by default.

Behavior under the new default

The following table summarizes how behavior changes for applications that do not explicitly configure auto.offset.reset or share.auto.offset.reset.

ScenarioOld behavior (latest)New behavior (by_duration:PT5S)
Brand-new group consuming an existing partition with substantial backlogSeek directly to the log endReplay only the most recent approximately 5 seconds
Partition expansion while the consumer is actively runningSilently skip records produced during the metadata-blindness windowStart at the beginning of the new partition because no records are older than 5 seconds
Offset out of range due to retention or deletionSeek directly to the log endResume from approximately 5 seconds before the reset time
Consumer offline for an extended period, then resumesSkip accumulated backlogConsume only recent data, approximately the last 5 seconds


The partition-expansion case is the primary motivation for this KIP. The new default replaces a silent correctness failure with a bounded replay window. Other reset scenarios remain intentionally bounded and predictable: instead of jumping to the log end, the consumer replays only a small amount of recent data.

Why PT5S

The duration must be long enough to cover the common partition-discovery window, but short enough that replay remains operationally negligible when a reset occurs.

During the KIP-1327 discussion, reviewers observed that a by_duration value in the 5–10 second range addresses the common partition-expansion problem, given the default heartbeat.interval.ms of 3 seconds. This KIP chooses PT5S, the lower end of that range, to minimize migration impact while still covering the common case.

For a running consumer, partition discovery is bounded by the heartbeat and assignment cadence of the group protocol.

ProtocolDefault heartbeat intervalConfig
Modern consumer group (KIP-848)5sgroup.consumer.heartbeat.interval.ms
Classic consumer group3sheartbeat.interval.ms
Share group (KIP-932)5sgroup.share.heartbeat.interval.ms


In the modern consumer group protocol and the share group protocol, the coordinator drives assignment updates on the heartbeat cadence. A partition created just after one heartbeat is therefore normally discovered on the next heartbeat, which is approximately one interval later under default settings.

PT5S covers this common case while keeping the replay window small. It matches the default heartbeat interval for the modern consumer group and share group protocols, exceeds the classic protocol's default heartbeat interval, and remains short enough that replay volume should be negligible for typical workloads.

This KIP intentionally chooses the lower end of the 5–10 second range rather than a larger value such as PT10S or PT30S:

  • A larger duration increases reprocessing whenever a reset occurs, including for brand-new groups, offset-out-of-range recovery, and consumers resuming after retention has advanced past their committed offsets.
  • Keeping the value small minimizes the migration impact for applications that previously relied on the implicit latest default.
  • The consumer's own poll() cadence and rebalance latency may add additional wall-clock buffer between partition discovery and consumption, so the effective protection window can be slightly wider than the raw duration.
  • Applications with stricter requirements can still set an explicit value, whether that means latest, earliest, none where supported, a shorter by_duration, or a longer by_duration.

The classic consumer protocol is being removed in Kafka 5.0 under KIP-1274, which coincides with this default change. This proposal therefore does not tune PT5S around classic-protocol-specific discovery behavior, including longer metadata-refresh paths. The default is targeted at the modern consumer group protocol and share groups.

Compatibility, Deprecation, and Migration Plan

This KIP introduces a behavioral change for applications that rely on the implicit latest default without explicitly configuring auto.offset.reset or share.auto.offset.reset.

After upgrading, whenever a reset occurs, these consumers will replay approximately the last five seconds of recent data rather than seeking directly to the log end offset. This affects reset scenarios such as brand-new groups, offset-out-of-range recovery, and consumers resuming after their committed offsets have fallen out of retention.

The behavioral impact is intentionally small and bounded. Applications that require the previous behavior can restore it by explicitly setting: auto.offset.reset=latestFor share groups, users can restore the previous behavior with: share.auto.offset.reset=latest.

Classic consumer protocol

The classic consumer protocol is being removed in Kafka 5.0 under KIP-1274, which coincides with this default change. This KIP therefore does not define any classic-protocol-specific behavior.

Rollout

  • The default change will take effect in a major release, targeting Kafka 5.0.
  • No deprecation cycle is required because no APIs or configuration values are being removed. The previous latest behavior remains fully supported as an explicit configuration value.
  • The release notes and upgrade documentation should call out the behavioral change for applications that rely on the implicit reset-policy default.

Test Plan

Unit tests will verify that the new default resolves to by_duration:PT5S for the consumer, Kafka Streams, and that explicit overrides still win. Integration tests will confirm the key end-to-end guarantee, a running consumer loses no records when a topic is expanded — across all three group types.

Rejected Alternatives

Introduce a new to_start_time policy (KIP-1282)

Concept:
Anchor reset operations to the consumer group's creation timestamp.

This was the approach explored by KIP-1282. A group-level creation timestamp provides an elegant way to handle partition expansion: when a new partition is discovered, the consumer can reset to the offset corresponding to the time the group was created.

Pros:

  • Provides a natural model for partition expansion.
  • Avoids skipping records produced to new partitions after the group was created.
  • Gives the reset policy a stable group-level anchor.

Cons:

  • Requires the cluster to persist and expose consumer group creation timestamps.
  • Introduces difficult semantics for offset-out-of-range handling.
  • Creates inconsistent behavior depending on whether group metadata still exists.
  • Makes reset behavior harder to explain to users.

The most contentious issue was offset-out-of-range behavior. Under the proposed design, a consumer with an out-of-range offset would reset to earliest if the group metadata still existed, but could reset to latest after the group metadata had been garbage-collected. Reviewers considered this difficult to reason about and inconsistent with the principle that backlog should be treated uniformly.

Add auto.offset.reset.new.partitions (KIP-1327)

Concept:
Introduce a separate reset policy that applies only to newly added partitions.

This was the approach explored by KIP-1327. The proposal introduced an auxiliary configuration, auto.offset.reset.new.partitions, together with server-side logic to distinguish newly added partitions from existing partitions.

Pros:

  • Provides explicit per-new-partition reset behavior.
  • Allows users to preserve latest for ordinary reset scenarios while choosing a safer policy for partition expansion.
  • Directly targets the partition-expansion race.

Cons:

Implementing this requires substantial protocol and metadata changes, including:

  • Persisting consumer group creation timestamps.
  • Modifying on-disk metadata record formats such as ConsumerGroupMetadataValue and PartitionRecord.
  • Introducing new metadata-version and group-version gates.
  • Extending GroupHeartbeatResponse with a NewPartitions field.
  • Defining behavior for share groups.
  • Addressing mirrored-cluster and replication-related edge cases.

This machinery is disproportionate to the common failure window, which is typically only a few seconds for actively running consumers under the modern group protocol.

results.title: KIP-1362: Add a rollback-compatible storage format option for KRaft migration

storage.value:
Status

Current state: Under Discussion

Discussion thread: here

Vote thread: here

JIRA: KAFKA-20762

Pull request (reference implementation): PR #22751

Please keep the discussion on the mailing list rather than commenting on the wiki (wiki discussions get unwieldy fast).

Motivation

The ZooKeeper-to-KRaft migration is designed so that a cluster can linger in the dual-write phase and roll back to ZooKeeper mode if an operator discovers a problem before the migration is finalized.

In production environments, at any point in time, hardware failures may happen, some of which are cause for replacing nodes, such as failing disks. Kafka fully supports node replacements out of the box.

These two aspects (node replacements/provisioning and KRaft migration rollback) are documented as orthogonal concepts.

However, it has been observed in production systems that node replacements during a KRaft migration, when following the documented procedures, breaks the ability to roll back. This is not documented, and as both mechanisms are important tooling for operators to keep clusters available, it's preferable to make them work in conjunction. There is no way to eliminate the risk of hardware failures during an ongoing migration, and as such, the sanctioned tooling needs to be adapted to handle them.

Today, when a broker is lost during the migration and the documented process for provisioning a replacement is followed, the replacement's storage is formatted using the kafka-storage.sh format procedure. That command unconditionally writes meta.properties with version=1. If a rollback is later required, the operator configures the brokers back into migration mode — at which point the newly provisioned broker rejects its own storage and crashes before becoming available:


The incompatibility is not documented, and node replacement is a routine operation for managed-fleet operators. The result is a silent loss of the rollback capability that the migration is supposed to preserve, discovered only at the worst possible time: during an attempted rollback.

The broker itself already formats empty log directories with a rollback-compatible version=0 meta.properties when it starts up in migration mode, so the capability exists in the code base. It is simply not reachable through the provisioning tool that operators are instructed to use. This KIP closes that gap.

Public Interfaces

A new optional flag is added to the format subcommand of the storage tool (bin/kafka-storage.sh format):

Help text: Format the node so that it remains compatible with rolling back an in-progress KRaft migration to ZooKeeper mode.

The flag is a boolean switch and takes no argument. When it is passed, the format command performs storage formatting identically to how the broker itself does during a migration sequence, resulting in a meta.properties with version=0. When it is omitted, the command behaves exactly as before and writes version=1.

No existing flags, defaults, output, exit codes, or other behaviors change.

Proposed Changes

When --zk-rollback-compatible is set, the storage tool selects MetaPropertiesVersion.V0 instead of the default MetaPropertiesVersion.V1 when building the meta.properties for each formatted log directory. This is the same version the broker writes for itself while it is in migration mode, so a node provisioned this way can participate in a rollback in exactly the way an original migration broker can.

This fix will be made on the 3.9 development branch only, as it is the only currently supported version that still supports ZooKeeper, and by extension the only supported version where KRaft migrations are still supported.

Documentation is updated in two places in the KRaft operations guide: a new "Formatting Nodes During a KRaft Migration" subsection under provisioning explains when and how to use the flag, and the migration-phases section links to it. The documentation makes clear that the flag is only relevant while a migration can still be rolled back, and should no longer be used once the migration has been finalized.

Compatibility, Deprecation, and Migration Plan

The change is fully backward compatible. The flag is opt-in, and omitting it preserves the current behavior byte-for-byte. No configuration, no other command line option, and no on-disk default is altered for existing users.

There is nothing to deprecate and no migration required. Operators who are not performing a ZooKeeper-to-KRaft migration have no reason to use the flag and are unaffected.

Test Plan

Unit tests assert both directions of the behavior at both layers that were changed:

  • The storage tool verifies that format --zk-rollback-compatible produces a version=0 meta.properties and that a plain format still produces version=1.
  • The underlying formatter verifies the same mapping when setZkRollbackCompatible(true) is set versus the default.

Rejected Alternatives

Document the incompatibility as intended behavior

We could declare that node replacement is unsupported while a migration is rollback-eligible and simply document that constraint. This was rejected because it removes a recovery path during an already high-risk operational mode and pushes significant operational burden onto operators, for no benefit — the capability already exists in the broker and is cheap to expose.

results.title: KIP-1363: Add --checkpoint option to kafka-metadata-shell and deprecate --snapshot

storage.value:
Status

Current state: Under Discussion

Discussion thread: here

JIRA: KAFKA-20668

Motivation

The kafka-metadata-shell tool exposes a option --snapshot to point at the file to read. The flag name is misleading: the metadata snapshot use the .checkpoint suffix, while kafka also has .snapshot files in log directory which are producer snapshots. This leads users to pass the wrong file.

This KIP proposes adding a --checkpoint option and deprecating --snapshot (keeping it as an alias for backward compatibility).

Public Interfaces

This KIP changes the command-line arguments of kafka-metadata-shell.sh.

A new option will be added: --checkpoint <path>. The existing options will remain supported as deprecated aliases: --snapshot <path>, -s <path>.

Example: bin/kafka-metadata-shell.sh --checkpoint metadata_log_dir/__cluster_metadata-0/00000000000000007228-0000000001.checkpoint 

Proposed Changes

Add --checkpoint as the preferred option for selecting the metadata checkpoint file.

Keep --snapshot and -s as deprecated aliases for compatibility. When either deprecated alias is used, the tool will print a deprecation warning recommending --checkpoint.

Only one of --checkpoint, --snapshot, or -s may be specified in a single invocation. The KRaft operations documentation will be updated to use --checkpoint.

Compatibility, Deprecation, and Migration Plan

This change is backward compatible.

Existing scripts using --snapshot or -s will continue to work, but users should migrate to --checkpoint.

This KIP does not remove --snapshot or -s. Any future removal should be handled separately.

There are no protocol changes, storage format changes, or broker-side behavior changes.

Test Plan

The change will be covered by metadata shell argument parsing tests and existing metadata shell integration tests.

The tests will verify that:

  • --checkpoint is accepted. 
  • --snapshot and -s remain accepted and emit a deprecation warning. 
  • using both the new option and a deprecated alias is rejected. 
  • invoking the tool without a checkpoint option is rejected. 
  • existing shell commands passed after the checkpoint file are preserved. 

Rejected Alternatives

results.title: KIP-1364: Expose Rebalance Cause to RebalanceConsumer and Metrics

storage.value:
Status

Current state: In Discussion

Discussion thread: here

JIRA: ASF JIRA5aa69414-a9e9-3523-82ec-879b028fb15bKAFKA-20788

Please keep the discussion on the mailing list rather than commenting on the wiki (wiki discussions get unwieldy fast).

Motivation

This is a follow-up from implementing KIP-1306. A Kafka consumer client today cannot tell why a rebalance happened without grepping logs. The rebalance trigger can help with triaging:

  • max.poll.interval.ms exceeded implies misconfig or delayed poll loop; last-polled-seconds-ago metric can help but only provide a trend, even a single event can trigger the consumer to leave.
  • Member fencing points at session timeout, GC pauses, or a duplicate group.instance.id.
  • Coordinator-initiated rebalances are regular occurrences due to join and leave requests, subscription changes, new topics resolved against a regex, assignors changed.
  • Application calls to Consumer.enforceRebalance() are expected and the application owns the context.

Existing rebalance metrics describe frequency and latency but carry no cause dimension:

rebalance-rate-per-hour, rebalance-latency-{avg,max}, rebalance-total
last-rebalance-seconds-ago, last-poll-seconds-ago

A spike in rebalance-rate-per-hour cannot be narrowed without consumer logs.

The classic protocol already captures the reason internally(AbstractCoordinator.rejoinReason, set on every requestRejoin call). It is consumed only as the JoinGroup request's reason field and dropped afterward.

Under the consumer protocol, the coordinator drives the rebalance and knows the cause when it bumps the group epoch; currently it only logs it and emits an opaque metric in coordinator-metrics: consumer-group-rebalance-rate/count.

Similar requests for this gap in observability have been made in KAFKA-12472 ; the JIRA requests for gauge client-side but after KIP-848 these have been moved broker-side. This KIP addresses the requirement but with broker/client side metrics and a new accessor in RebalanceConsumer, the callback introduced in KIP-1306.

Public Interfaces

RebalanceCause

javaRebalanceCause= 0; } /** This cause's bit in the {@code AssignmentCauses} bitmask; valid only when {@link #onWire()}. */ public short wireBit() { return (short) (1 << code); } /** Human-readable description, for logging. Wording is not guaranteed stable across releases. */ public String message() { return message; } // Reverse lookup built from the code field (order-independent, never ordinal); fails fast on a duplicate. private static final RebalanceCause[] BY_CODE = new RebalanceCause[Short.SIZE]; static { for (RebalanceCause c : values()) if (c.onWire()) { if (BY_CODE[c.code] != null) throw new IllegalStateException("duplicate code " + c.code); BY_CODE[c.code] = c; } } /** The coordinator-origin cause for a wire bit index, or {@link #UNKNOWN} if unrecognized. */ public static RebalanceCause fromCode(int code) { return (code >= 0 && code < BY_CODE.length && BY_CODE[code] != null) ? BY_CODE[code] : UNKNOWN; } }]]>

On the consumer protocol every value can occur except USER_REQUESTED (enforceRebalance is a no-op there). On classic, MEMBER_JOINED / MEMBER_REMOVED / ASSIGNOR_CHANGED do not occur (folded into COORDINATOR_INITIATED).

Additions to RebalanceConsumer

javaRebalanceConsumer


cause shares the existing callback-scoped lifecycle: calling it after the enclosing rebalance callback returns throws IllegalStateException, consistent with all other methods on RebalanceConsumer

AssignmentCauses field on ConsumerGroupHeartbeatResponse

jsonAssignmentCauses

A bitmask of the different assignment states for this group between the groupEpoch and memberEpoch OR'd with each other.

Bits 0-5 correspond to enums MEMBER_JOINED to REGEX_MATCHED_TOPIC in RebalanceCause with COORDINATOR_INITIATED as a generic catch-all state.

BitRebalanceCause
1<<0MEMBER_JOINED
1<<1MEMBER_REMOVED
1<<2SUBSCRIPTION_CHANGED
1<<3TOPIC_METADATA_CHANGED
1<<4ASSIGNOR_CHANGED
1<<5REGEX_MATCHED_TOPIC
1<<6COORDINATOR_INITIATED (generic/unclassified)

Proposed Changes

In the consumer protocol, epoch increments and the heartbeat response are async, so the classic approach of request to rebalance cause does not cleanly apply. Many members could send their heartbeat requests any of which can trigger a new assignment causing partition add/revoke on the consumer. A lagging member adopts the latest target assignment and skips the intermediate state changes between epochs from the last heartbeat. Therefore, a single coordinator reason does not fit the real "cause" of a rebalance for that particular member. To let the consumer client calculate the intermediate states, we return a bit mask of each state from the last member epoch to the current group epoch. We only include the reasons in a heartbeat response when the member indeed needs a new assignment - which is the real trigger for a rebalance to be triggered on the client anyway.

Coordinator

Each protocol resolves the cause at its epoch-bump site and records the per-cause broker metric there specifically in GroupMetadataManager.java. Note: The member-removal bump records no rebalance sensor today, so this KIP adds the call (labelled MEMBER_REMOVED) at consumerGroupFenceMembers.

For the consumer wire bitmask the coordinator holds a per-group transient ring of rebalance cause bits on GroupMetadataManager: a Map<String, short[]> keyed by group id (short[N], N = 512, ~1 KB/group). This is best-effort in-memory state rather than replayed records since rebalance events are by nature unorganised; there is no persistent memory of the order of events. At each epoch-bump site the coordinator writes the bump's cause bits to ring[groupEpoch mod N]: updateSubscriptionMetadata (subscription / regex / assignor / metadata, or MEMBER_JOINED for a new member), the async regex-resolution job (REGEX_MATCHED_TOPIC), and consumerGroupFenceMembers (MEMBER_REMOVED). The ring is dropped with the group in removeGroup. A heartbeat response to set the AssignmentCauses ORs the window between memberEpoch and groupEpoch.

We return UNKNOWN if the width is greater than N so as to not track very long history. N exceeds the epochs bumpable within a session.timeout.ms, so a live member is inside the ring (one lagging past it is about to be fenced). Being best-effort in-memory state, the ring is empty on a new coordinator after failover (members read UNKNOWN until it refills), and as with the rebalance-count sensor recorded at the same sites.

The bitmask union tends to be overinclusive i.e. it may name a coordinator cause that did not move this member specifically (the coordinator only computes the latest target) - the client will resolve this to COORDINATOR_INITIATED but emit all the intermediate states that caused the new assignment. When multiple members join/leave between the heartbeat under churn, it is difficult to pinpoint which particular event triggered the rebalance for this member.

For instance, between the heartbeat request for m1, two other member actors m2, m3 can interact before the HB response goes out. If m2 leaves the group, m3 begins a subscription_changed : the current behaviour is to set the new assignment caused by m2 leaving (member_removed) but if we were to choose only the latest trigger (subscription_changed) we can misattribute the cause of the rebalance as subscription_changed. The broker will correctly emit a metric at each rebalance event for each cause, but the client only sees an aggregated view at the response. This is an acceptable lack of precision in timing with minimal data transfer.

The new assignment is returned on the heartbeat response only if that member is affected (new member, assignment change) - so other members' HB response do not contain the causes bitmask.

Both the client and coordinator log cause.message() for a consistent token; the coordinator can append member id, epoch, and context to the message.

Client Metrics

rebalance-rate-per-hour and rebalance-total are unchanged; a new cause-tagged pair is added in the consumer-coordinator-metrics group (kafka.consumer:type=consumer-coordinator-metrics,client-id=([-.\w]+)):

MetricTagSemantics
rebalance-cause-totalcauseIncidence count per cause
rebalance-cause-rate-per-hourcauseIncidence rate per cause

A multi-cause rebalance increments each cause, so sum(rebalance-cause-total{cause=*}) can exceed rebalance-total (new names keep existing dashboards intact).

Cause label values are the lower-case enum names. Total cardinality per consumer is bounded at 14 i.e. one per enum value.

As noted above, if there are multiple triggers between the member epoch and group epoch at the next heartbeat, then we emit one metric per cause but export COORDINATOR_INITIATED to the RebalanceListener callback.

Broker Metrics

Register new metrics with an additional cause tag to the group-coordinator-metrics existing consumer-group-rebalance-count/rate metrics. Each Coordinator originated rebalance cause listed above in the AssignmentCauses section is a label, so the cardinality is at 7 per metric.

MetricAdded tagDescription
consumer-group-rebalance-rate/countcauseExisting metric, now also published per cause

Out of scope

  • Client cause() for Streams and Share. StreamsRebalanceListener has no RebalanceConsumer-style context and Share has no application-facing rebalance callback. Left to a follow-up KIP.
  • Broker metrics for share-group-rebalance-* metrics. Also left as follow-on work.

Compatibility, Deprecation, and Migration Plan

  • One new enum and related addition of one method to RebalanceConsumer. The interface's only intended implementer is the consumer's internal delegate, so applications using RebalanceListener (or the legacy ConsumerRebalanceListener that extends it) are unaffected unless they read cause().
  • JMX Metrics Reporter: The cause-tagged metrics are registered alongside the existing untagged metrics; queries against the untagged names are unaffected.
  • Legacy ConsumerRebalanceListener. The one-arg callback signatures do not receive a RebalanceConsumer and therefore cannot read cause. This is intentional. Applications that want cause must migrate to RebalanceListener

Test Plan

  • Unit tests mapping each requestRejoin call site to the expected RebalanceCause.
  • Unit tests for fencing across the classic error codes and the Consumer group protocol codes.
  • Unit tests for cause() lifecycle (IllegalStateException after callback return).
  • Unit tests for per-cause metric registration and bounded cardinality - client and broker.
  • Coordinator: each bump maps to the expected cause and records the metric, including the added call at consumerGroupFenceMembers.
  • Integration tests for the full lifecycle for each cause listed above.

Rejected Alternatives

Single latest-cause scalar on the wire. Noted in Coordinator section above, chances of misattribution because of cause when multiple members interact during the window between memberEpoch - groupEpoch.

KAFKA-12472's enum status gauge. KIP-848 moved the decision server-side (the client can't populate a gauge without protocol change), and highest-wins needs an arbitrary ranking and cannot express co-occurring causes (see above point).

Fine-grained enum with one value per internal trigger: Considered more granular values. The surface grows with every internal refactor, applications cannot reasonably switch over many cases, and finer metric granularity is not desirable due to larger cardinality.

A causes() set accessor. Needless surface and confusing; applications watch cause rather than branch on it, so the set lives in the metric

Free-form String cause instead of an enum: Flexible reasoning but forces applications to parse strings to switch on cause and defeats metric tagging. Also, the cardinality goes unbounded.

Introduce a separate RebalanceContext interface: Considered amending KIP-1306 so the listener callbacks take a new RebalanceContext exposing consumer(), cause(), and causeMessage(). Rejected because KIP-1306 settled on RebalanceConsumer as the second-argument type on its RebalanceListener callbacks. Future additions (epoch, member id, server-side reason) can land on RebalanceConsumer directly.

Three-argument listener overload: Adds cause as a third callback parameter rather than as a method on RebalanceConsumer. Related to the same KIP above, RebalanceConsumer serves as the natural extension point.

results.title: KIP-1365: Transform Observability and Skipped Record Handling for Kafka Connect

storage.value:
Status

Current state: "Under Discussion"

Discussion thread: here 

JIRA: here 

Please keep the discussion on the mailing list rather than commenting on the wiki (wiki discussions get unwieldy fast).

Motivation

Kafka Connect's Single Message Transform (SMT) framework allows users to build chains of transformations that process records between the connector and Kafka. Transforms can modify records, route them to different topics, or drop them entirely by returning null (a filter operation). When combined with the error tolerance framework (errors.tolerance=all), records can also be diverted to a Dead Letter Queue (DLQ) before reaching the connector.

Today, the transform layer has two significant gaps: no operational observability and no mechanism for sink connectors to learn about records they never received. This KIP addresses both with two complementary enhancements.

Problem 1: No Per-Transform Operational Metrics

Kafka Connect provides no operational metrics at the transform layer. The existing connector-transform-metrics group only exposes static metadata:


Existing MetricTypeDescription
transform-classGauge (string)The class name of the transformation
transform-versionGauge (string)The version of the transformation

This creates several operational pain points:

  1. No visibility into filtering — When using the Filter transform (or any transform that drops records by returning null), operators have no way to know how many records are being filtered. The only workaround is subtracting task-level source-record-poll-total from source-record-write-total (or sink-record-read-total from sink-record-send-total), which provides only an aggregate across the entire transform chain.
  2. No per-transform throughput — In a chain of 3-5 transforms, operators cannot determine the throughput contribution or bottleneck of each individual transform. If a transform has a bug that silently drops records, it goes undetected.
  3. No error attribution — While task-error-metrics tracks aggregate errors, operators cannot determine which transform in a chain is causing failures without correlating with debug-level logs.
  4. Capacity planning gap — Without per-transform record counts, operators cannot make informed decisions about whether a transform is cost-effective (e.g., "is this filter dropping 90% of records, or 1%?").

The consumer group protocol and other Kafka subsystems have rich per-component metrics. The transform layer is a notable gap.

Problem 2: Offset Gap for Sink Connectors When Records Are Skipped

The SinkTask.preCommit() API allows sink connectors to control which offsets are committed to Kafka. Many production connectors override this method to implement exactly-once or at-least-once delivery guarantees with external systems. These connectors track offsets based on records they receive in put() and only return offsets from preCommit() after durably writing to the external system.

When transforms or error tolerance drop records before put(), these connectors have no visibility into the dropped records. The result:

  1. Offset gap — The consumer position advances past the dropped records, but the sink's committed offset does not include them.
  2. Reprocessing after rebalance — On rebalance, the consumer seeks to the last committed offset and re-fetches the dropped records. The transforms drop them again, and the cycle repeats.
  3. Infinite reprocessing loop — If all records for a partition are dropped, the sink returns an empty map from preCommit(), the framework skips commit entirely, and no progress is ever made for that partition.

This problem affects widely-used connectors in production:


ConnectorOffset StrategyImpact
S3 SinkReturns offsets only after flushing to S3 (rotation interval / record count)Filtered records create offset gaps. Rebalance reprocesses all records since last S3 flush
IcebergSinkConnectorWorkers commit offset only after coordinator signalTrailing filtered records never committed. Gap grows with each poll cycle
Any connector using preCommit() returning {}Full offset opt-outIf all records filtered, partition offset permanently frozen

How the Two Problems Relate

The two problems form a diagnose → fix pair:



Without Part A, operators cannot diagnose where records are being dropped. Without Part B, connectors cannot act on records they never received. Together, they provide complete observability and correctness for the transform pipeline.

The use of SMTs and Predicates in production has grown significantly since their introduction. Common patterns that trigger these problems:

  • Filter SMT — Drop records not matching criteria (e.g., filter by record type, tenant, region)
  • RegexRouter + Predicate — Route and filter based on content
  • errors.tolerance=all — Tolerate conversion errors, send to DLQ
  • HeaderFilter + Predicate — Drop records missing required headers
  • Multi-tenant pipelines — Filter per-tenant records across shared topics

Success Criteria

AreaCriterion
ObservabilityOperators can query per-transform record-in, record-out, and record-filtered counts via JMX
ObservabilityOperators can compute per-transform filter rates for alerting and dashboards
CorrectnessSink connectors that override preCommit() can track offsets for all consumed records, including those dropped before put()
SafetyZero risk of data loss — the framework never overrides the sink's offset decisions
CompatibilityFull backward compatibility — existing connectors work identically without code changes
PerformanceZero performance regression for connectors with no transforms configured
UniversalityMetrics are available for all transforms (built-in and custom) without any transform code changes
SimplicityConnectors need minimal code changes to incorporate skipped record awareness

New or Changed Public Interfaces

  • New SkipReason Enum Types

    • Module: connect/api

TypePackageDescription
SkipReasonorg.apache.kafka.connect.sinkEnum: FILTERED, ERROR_TOLERATED
    • Full definition:
The record was NOT sent to the dead letter queue. */ FILTERED, /** * The record encountered an error during conversion or transformation, * the error was tolerated ({@code errors.tolerance=all}), and the * original record was sent to the dead letter queue. * *

The record was successfully written to the DLQ topic (or will be * before the next offset commit, as the framework awaits DLQ futures * before committing). */ ERROR_TOLERATED }]]>


  • New Public API: SinkTask.onRecordSkipped():

    • Module: connect/api
    • File: org.apache.kafka.connect.sink.SinkTask
    • Full signature and Javadoc:


This occurs when: *
    *
  • A {@link org.apache.kafka.connect.transforms.Transformation Transformation} * or {@link org.apache.kafka.connect.transforms.predicates.Predicate Predicate} * drops the record by returning {@code null} * ({@link SkipReason#FILTERED FILTERED}).
    • *
  • A conversion or transformation error is tolerated * ({@code errors.tolerance=all}) and the record is sent to the dead letter * queue ({@link SkipReason#ERROR_TOLERATED ERROR_TOLERATED}).
    • *
* *

When to override

* *

Sink tasks that override {@link #preCommit(Map)} and track offsets internally * (rather than using the framework-provided {@code currentOffsets}) should * override this method to incorporate skipped record offsets into their tracking. * Without this, a gap can form between the committed offset and the consumer * position, causing unnecessary reprocessing of skipped records after a rebalance. * *

When not to override

* *

Sink tasks that use the default {@link #preCommit(Map)} implementation (which * returns the framework-provided {@code currentOffsets}) do not need to * override this method. The framework's {@code currentOffsets} already accounts * for skipped records. * *

Threading

* *

This method is called on the same thread as {@link #put(Collection)}, during * the conversion and transformation phase of the poll loop. It is called once per * skipped record, before the corresponding batch's {@link #put(Collection)} call. * Implementations must not block. * *

Ordering guarantees

* *

Within a single poll batch, {@code onRecordSkipped()} calls are interleaved * with the conversion of other records in offset order. All {@code onRecordSkipped()} * calls for a batch complete before the batch's {@link #put(Collection)} call. * *

Error handling

* *

If this method throws an exception, the framework logs a warning, increments * the {@code sink-record-skip-callback-error} metric, and continues processing. * The exception does not affect record delivery or offset management. * Implementations should handle their own errors internally. * * @param partition the original Kafka topic partition of the skipped record * @param offset the original Kafka offset of the skipped record * @param reason why the record was skipped * @since 4.1 */ public void onRecordSkipped(TopicPartition partition, long offset, SkipReason reason) { // Default no-op. // Connectors using the default preCommit() do not need to override this. } }]]>

  • onRecordSkipped Method

    • The onRecordSkipped(TopicPartition, long, SkipReason) method is declared as a default no-op on SinkTask in New or Changed Public Interfaces → SinkTask API Changes. Sink tasks that override preCommit() and track offsets internally should override it to fold skipped-record offsets into their tracking. See that section for the full signature and Javadoc.

  • API Design Rationale

DecisionRationale
Default method (no-op)Backward compatible — existing connectors compile and work without changes
TopicPartition+ long offsetparametersMatches the granularity of preCommit(Map<TopicPartition, OffsetAndMetadata>). The sink needs partition and offset to update its tracking
SkipReasonenumSinks may want to log, metric, or handle filter vs DLQ differently. Extensible for future skip reasons
No SinkRecordparameterThe record may have failed conversion — a valid SinkRecord may not exist. Partition + offset is the minimum viable information
Called per-record, not batchedSimpler contract. Sinks that want batching can accumulate internally
Called before put()Sink can merge skipped offsets with delivered offsets in a single pass
Exceptions caught by frameworkNotification is advisory — a bug in onRecordSkipped()must not break the pipeline

  • Framework Integration: WorkerSinkTask Changes

    • The change to WorkerSinkTask is minimal — a single notification call in the existing else branch of convertMessages():
msgs) { for (ConsumerRecord msg : msgs) { log.trace("{} Consuming and converting message in topic '{}' partition {} at offset {} and timestamp {}", this, msg.topic(), msg.partition(), msg.offset(), msg.timestamp()); ProcessingContext> context = new ProcessingContext<>(msg); SinkRecord transRecord = convertAndTransformRecord(context, msg); TopicPartition tp = new TopicPartition(msg.topic(), msg.partition()); origOffsets.put(tp, new OffsetAndMetadata(msg.offset() + 1)); if (transRecord != null) { messageBatch.add(transRecord); } else { SkipReason reason = context.failed() ? SkipReason.ERROR_TOLERATED : SkipReason.FILTERED; try { task.onRecordSkipped(tp, msg.offset(), reason); } catch (Exception e) { log.warn("{} SinkTask.onRecordSkipped() threw an exception for " + "topic '{}' partition {} at offset {}: {}", this, msg.topic(), msg.partition(), msg.offset(), e.getMessage(), e); sinkTaskMetricsGroup.recordSkipCallbackError(); } sinkTaskMetricsGroup.recordSkippedRecord(reason); log.trace( "{} Record skipped ({}) in topic '{}' partition {} at offset {}", this, reason, msg.topic(), msg.partition(), msg.offset() ); } } sinkTaskMetricsGroup.recordConsumedOffsets(origOffsets); }]]>

  • Changes Summary

LocationChange
convertMessages()else branchAdd onRecordSkipped()call with try/catch
SinkTaskMetricsGroupAdd skip counters by reason
No changes to commitOffsets()Framework offset logic unchanged
No changes to deliverMessages()Delivery logic unchanged
No changes to preCommit() callSink retains full control


  • New JMX Metrics: Per-Transform

    • Six new attributes added to the existing connector-transform-metrics MBean:
    • MBean: kafka.connect:type=connector-transform-metrics,connector={name},task={id},transform={alias}
Metric NameTypeDescription
transform-record-in-ratedoubleRecords/second entering this transform
transform-record-in-totaldoubleTotal records entering this transform
transform-record-out-ratedoubleRecords/second produced by this transform
transform-record-out-totaldoubleTotal records produced by this transform
transform-record-filtered-ratedoubleRecords/second filtered (dropped) by this transform
transform-record-filtered-totaldoubleTotal records filtered (dropped) by this transform

  • New JMX Metrics: Task-Level Skipped Records

    • Eight new attributes added to the existing sink-task-metrics MBean:
    • MBean: kafka.connect:type=sink-task-metrics,connector={name},task={id}
Metric NameTypeDescription
sink-record-skipped-totaldoubleTotal records skipped (all reasons)
sink-record-skipped-ratedoubleRecords skipped per second
sink-record-filtered-totaldoubleRecords dropped by transforms/predicates
sink-record-filtered-ratedoubleFiltered records per second
sink-record-error-tolerated-totaldoubleRecords sent to DLQ via error tolerance
sink-record-error-tolerated-ratedoubleError-tolerated records per second
sink-record-skip-callback-error-totaldoubleTotal exceptions thrown by a connector's onRecordSkipped()override
sink-record-skip-callback-error-ratedoubleonRecordSkipped()exceptions per second

  • New Metric Templates

    • Fourteen new MetricNameTemplate fields in ConnectMetricsRegistry:


  • Internal Changes (Not Public API)

LocationModuleChange
TransformationChain.javaconnect/runtimeinitializeMetrics()method, instrumented apply() loop
WorkerTask.javaconnect/runtimeSensor creation in TaskMetricsGroup
WorkerSinkTask.javaconnect/runtime

onRecordSkipped()call in convertMessages(), SinkTaskMetricsGroupsensors, skip-callback-error sensor


  • No Wire Protocol Changes

    • This KIP does not introduce any new APIs, request/response schemas, or record types.

  • No Configuration Changes

    • No new broker or worker configuration properties are introduced. The metrics are automatically available for all connectors with transforms configured. The notification API is automatically available for all sink connectors.

Proposed Changes

  • Overview

    • This KIP introduces three complementary enhancements to Kafka Connect's transform pipeline:

      • Part A: Per-Transform Operational Metrics:

        • Six new JMX metrics per transform stage (records-in, records-out, records-filtered as counts and rates), recorded in TransformationChain.apply(). These provide per-transform visibility into record flow, including filter rates, for both source and sink connectors.

      • Part B: Skipped Record Notification API:

        • A new SinkTask.onRecordSkipped(TopicPartition, long, SkipReason) callback that notifies sink connectors about records consumed from Kafka but dropped before put(). This gives connectors the information they need to make correct offset decisions in preCommit(), closing the offset gap caused by filtered and DLQ'd records.

      • Part C: Task-Level Skipped Record Metrics:

        • Eight new JMX metrics at the sink task level (skipped-total, filtered-total, error-tolerated-total, and skip-callback-error as counts and rates), recorded when records are dropped in WorkerSinkTask.convertMessages().

    • Key Design Principle:

      • Inform, don't decide. The framework gives operators and connectors the complete picture. The sink retains full authority over offset management.
    • This principle was chosen over framework-level automatic offset advancement (see Rejected Alternatives) because the framework cannot safely predict the sink's internal state — whether it has un-flushed buffers, pending transactions, or other reasons to hold back offset commits.

  • Detailed Design

    • Part A: Per-Transform Operational Metrics

      • New Transform Metrics
      • For each transform alias in a connector's transforms configuration, the following sensors are created:
      • Records In — Incremented once for every record that enters the transform stage. This includes records where the predicate evaluates to false and the transform is skipped (the record still "entered" the stage).
      • Records Out — Incremented once for every record that exits the transform stage with a non-null result.
      • Records Filtered — Incremented once for every record that is dropped by the transform stage (null return from TransformationStage.apply() or null return from RetryWithToleranceOperator due to a tolerated error).
      • Invariant: For any transform stage over any time window( Except when the exception is thrown by the transform / converter): records-in = records-out + records-filtered


      • Instrumentation Point
        • The metrics are recorded in TransformationChain.apply(), which is the central execution point for all transforms in both source and sink tasks.
        • Current code (no instrumentation):
context, R record) { if (transformationStages.isEmpty()) return record; for (final TransformationStage transformationStage : transformationStages) { final R current = record; record = retryWithToleranceOperator.execute( context, () -> transformationStage.apply(current), Stage.TRANSFORMATION, transformationStage.transformClass()); if (record == null) break; } return record; }]]>


        • Proposed code (with instrumentation):
context, R record) { if (transformationStages.isEmpty()) return record; for (int i = 0; i < transformationStages.size(); i++) { final TransformationStage transformationStage = transformationStages.get(i); final R current = record; recordSensorValue(i, RECORDS_IN_INDEX); record = retryWithToleranceOperator.execute( context, () -> transformationStage.apply(current), Stage.TRANSFORMATION, transformationStage.transformClass()); if (record == null) { recordSensorValue(i, RECORDS_FILTERED_INDEX); break; } else { recordSensorValue(i, RECORDS_OUT_INDEX); } } return record; }]]>


      • Metric Semantics
Scenariorecords-inrecords-outrecords-filtered
Transform passes record through unchanged110
Transform modifies and returns record110
Transform returns null (filter)101
Predicate is false, transform skipped110
Transform throws, error tolerated (null)101
Transform throws, error not tolerated100 (exception propagates)

        • Note on predicate-skipped records:
          • When a predicate causes the transform to be skipped, TransformationStage.apply()returns the original record unchanged. From the chain's perspective, the record entered and exited the stage — it counts as records-in and records-out. This is the correct semantic because the stage did process the record (it evaluated the predicate and decided to pass it through).
        • Note on tolerated errors:

    • Part B: Skipped Record Notification API

      • Problem Analysis
        • The offset gap occurs because of a responsibility mismatch in the sink pipeline:


        • The framework applies transforms and drops records, but the sink — which is responsible for authorizing offset commits — has no knowledge that those records existed.

The onRecordSkipped() notification is orthogonal — it is called during convertMessages(), well before commitOffsets(). The two mechanisms are independent and do not interfere.

Compatibility, Deprecation, and Migration Plan

  • Backward Compatibility
    • This KIP is fully backward compatible:

Existing metricsNo existing metrics are removed or renamed
New metricsPurely additive — appear automatically after upgrade
Wire protocolNo changes

Connect REST APINo changes
Monitoring dashboardsExisting dashboards are unaffected. New dashboards can be built using the new metrics


  • Connector Migration Guide
    • Step 1: Identify If You need to override these new api’s
      • Your connector might need these new api’s if ALL of the following are true:
        1. You override preCommit() (or flush() if preCommit() calls it and returns custom offsets)
        2. Your preCommit() returns offsets based on records received in put()
        3. Your users configure SMTs, Predicates that filter records, or errors.tolerance=all
    • Step 2: Add onRecordSkipped Override
skippedHighWatermarks = new HashMap<>(); @Override public void onRecordSkipped(TopicPartition partition, long offset, SkipReason reason) { skippedHighWatermarks.merge(partition, offset + 1, Math::max); }]]>


    • Step 3: Incorporate into preCommit
      • Choose the pattern that matches your connector's flush behavior:
        • Immediate flush (Pattern 2): Merge skippedHighWatermarks directly into returned offsets
        • Buffered flush (Pattern 3): Only advance for partitions with no pending data OR after successful flush
        • Transaction-based: Include skipped offsets in the same transaction boundary

    • Step 4: Clear State on Partition Close
partitions) { partitions.forEach(skippedHighWatermarks::remove); // ... existing cleanup ... }]]>


    • Step 5: Test
      • Verify with a Filter SMT that drops a high percentage of records. Trigger a rebalance and confirm no reprocessing of filtered records.

Test Plan

  • Part A: Transform Metrics Tests


TestDescription

  • Part B: Skipped Record Notification Tests

    • Unit Tests

Test ClassTest FocusKey Assertions

    • Integration Tests
Test ScenarioSetupKey Assertion
Custom preCommit with onRecordSkippedConnector tracks skipped offsets, Filter SMT drops 50%After rebalance, no reprocessing of filtered records
All records filtered for one partitionTwo partitions, one fully filteredFiltered partition offset advances; other partition unaffected
