    • Parameterized Test Matrix
      • Each integration test should be parameterized across:

        • SMT type: Filter, RegexRouter with predicate, custom transform returning null
        • Error tolerance: errors.tolerance=none (DLQ path not tested), errors.tolerance=all
        • preCommit style: default, custom returning partial offsets, custom returning empty map
        • Connector: with onRecordSkipped override, without override (baseline)

Rejected Alternatives

Alternative 1: Framework Offset Floor

Approach: The framework tracks skipped record offsets internally and enforces a minimum "floor" offset during commitOffsets(). Even when the sink returns custom offsets from preCommit(), the framework would advance the committed offset to at least the skipped record floor.

Why rejected:

The framework cannot safely determine when advancing the offset is safe. Consider the S3 Sink Connector:

  1. Records 0-49 delivered to sink, 50-100 filtered
  2. S3 Sink buffers records 0-49, hasn't flushed to S3 yet
  3. preCommit() returns {} — "not ready to commit"
  4. Framework floor would commit offset 101
  5. S3 flush later fails — records 0-49 permanently lost

The fundamental problem: the framework doesn't know the sink's internal state. The sink's preCommit() return value is a deliberate signal about what's safe to commit, not an oversight. Any framework-level override risks data loss for connectors with complex flush/commit semantics.

Even a "smart" floor that only advances for partitions where the sink received no records can fail in edge cases:

  • A connector might use preCommit() → {} as a global "hold everything" signal across all partitions
  • A connector might have cross-partition transactional semantics
  • A connector might coordinate offset commits with an external system's transaction

The notification approach is strictly safer: it gives the sink complete information and lets it make the decision, eliminating all framework-side risk.

Alternative 2: Separate Callbacks per Skip Reason

Approach: Two separate methods: onFilteredRecord(TopicPartition, long) for transform drops and onDlqRecord(TopicPartition, long)for DLQ diversions.

Why rejected:

  • Same offset tracking logic — From the sink's perspective, both cases have identical offset management needs. Two callbacks means duplicated logic in every connector implementation.
  • API surface — One method with an enum parameter is cleaner than two methods doing the same thing.
  • Extensibility — If new skip reasons are added in the future (e.g., record size limits, schema validation), a new enum value is backward compatible; a new method is not.
  • Precedent — The SkipReason enum allows sinks that DO care about the distinction to branch on it.

Alternative 3: Enriching the preCommit Parameter

Approach: Change the preCommit(Map<TopicPartition, OffsetAndMetadata>) signature to include metadata about which offsets correspond to skipped records. For example, preCommit(Map<TopicPartition, OffsetAndMetadata>, Map<TopicPartition, List<Long>> skippedOffsets).

Why rejected:

  • Breaks backward compatibility — Changing preCommit() signature is a source-incompatible change. All existing connectors would need to update.
  • Overloading — Adding an overload with extra parameters is confusing and hard to deprecate.
  • Wrong abstraction — preCommit() is about committing; skip notification is about record-level awareness. Mixing them creates an API that's hard to reason about.
  • Timing — Skip information is available during conversion (in convertMessages()), but preCommit() is called much later. The sink should learn about skips as they happen, not retroactively.

Alternative 4: Automatic Offset Advancement with Configuration

Approach: Add a connector config transforms.offset.commit.policy=framework|connector that controls whether the framework automatically commits offsets for skipped records.

Why rejected (as a standalone solution):

  • Data loss risk — Even with careful case analysis (see Alternative 1), the framework cannot guarantee safety for all sink implementations. A configuration option that enables data-loss-prone behavior shifts blame to operators.
  • Complexity — Requires the framework to track filteredOffsets, lastDeliveredOffsets, and implement multi-case floor logic. This complexity is unnecessary if the sink is simply informed.
  • Still needs notification — Even with this config, connectors that want correct behavior with policy=connector need the notification API anyway. So this alternative is additive, not a replacement.

However, this could be reconsidered as a future enhancement layered on top of the notification API, specifically for the narrow case where all records for a partition are filtered and the sink has no data at risk.

Alternative 5: SinkTaskContext Extension

Approach: Add a method to SinkTaskContext (e.g., context.skippedOffsets()) that the sink can query during preCommit() to discover which offsets were skipped.

Why rejected:

  • Polling vs notification — Forces the sink to remember to check during preCommit(). Easy to forget, easy to get wrong. A callback is harder to miss in code review.
  • State management ambiguity — When does skippedOffsets() reset? After preCommit()? After commit succeeds? The lifecycle is unclear.
  • Same information, worse ergonomics — The notification approach pushes information to the sink at the right time. The context approach requires the sink to pull it at the right time.

Alternative 6: Per-Transform Latency Metrics

Approach: Adding transform-record-latency-avg and transform-record-latency-max per transform.

Why rejected: While useful for identifying slow transforms, it was deferred to keep this KIP focused on record counting and the offset gap fix. Latency metrics can be added in a follow-up KIP using the same infrastructure (adding Avg and Maxstats to the same MetricGroup instances).

Alternative 7: Separate Metric Group for Transform Operational Metrics

Approach: Creating a new connector-transform-operation-metrics group separate from the existing connector-transform-metricsmetadata group.

Why rejected:

  • Fragments the JMX namespace — operators would need to look in two places
  • The existing group already has per-transform tags and cardinality
  • Kafka's convention is to co-locate all metrics for a component in one group

Alternative 8: Instrumenting Inside TransformationStage

Approach: Placing the metric recording inside TransformationStage.apply() instead of TransformationChain.apply().

Why rejected:

  • TransformationStage doesn't have visibility into whether RetryWithToleranceOperator tolerates an error (which also produces a null return)
  • The chain is the natural orchestration point that sees the final outcome of each stage
  • Avoids coupling TransformationStage to the metrics framework

Alternative 9: Implementing Metrics via the Monitorable Interface

Approach: Having individual Transformation implementations opt into metrics via the Monitorable interface.

Why rejected:

  • Requires every transform (including third-party) to implement metrics
  • Cannot capture chain-level semantics (filtered vs error-tolerated)
  • Inconsistent coverage — built-in transforms would have metrics, third-party would not
  • The chain-level approach provides uniform coverage with zero transform code changes

results.title: KIP-1366: Configurable Segment Interval for Window and Session Stores

storage.value:
Status

Current state: Under Discussion

Discussion thread: here 

JIRA: here

Please keep the discussion on the mailing list rather than commenting on the wiki (wiki discussions get unwieldy fast).

Motivation

Kafka Streams window and session state stores are internally divided into time-based segments, each backed by a separate RocksDB instance. The segment interval controls how wide each segment is in time. Currently, the segment interval for window and session stores is computed automatically as max(retentionPeriod / 2, 60_000ms) and is not configurable through the public API.

This creates two problems:

  1. Changing retention requires a full state store restore.
    Because the segment interval is derived from the retention period, any change to retention also changes the segment boundaries. Since segment boundaries determine the on-disk directory structure and key layout, a retention change invalidates the existing state store data and requires restoring from the changelog topic. This is unnecessarily disruptive — a user who simply wants to keep data longer or shorter should not have to pay the cost of a full restore.
  2. The default segment size is suboptimal for common access patterns.
    Many streaming applications need a long retention or grace period (e.g., 7 days) but access recent data the vast majority of the time. With the current formula, a 7-day retention produces segments of ~3.5 days. This means the active segment — the one receiving all writes and most reads — is very large, leading to heavier RocksDB compaction and lower cache-hit ratios. A user who knows their access pattern could benefit from smaller segments (e.g., 1 hour), keeping the active segment compact while still retaining historical data across many smaller segments.

Notably, Stores.persistentVersionedKeyValueStore already accepts an optional segmentInterval parameter, introduced in KIP-889: Versioned State Stores. KIP-889 established both the API pattern and the rationale for user-configurable segments. This KIP extends the same capability to window and session stores, where the internal plumbing already supports a configurable segment interval — it is simply not exposed in the public API.

Public Interfaces

New method overloads in `org.apache.kafka.streams.state.Stores`

Window stores


java

Session stores

java

Validation

The following constraints are enforced on segmentInterval:

  • Must be at least 60,000 milliseconds (1 minute). This matches the minimum already used by the default formula (max(retentionPeriod / 2, 60_000ms)). Segments smaller than 1 minute would create an excessive number of RocksDB instances for any practical retention period.
  • For window stores: must be greater than or equal to windowSize. A segment smaller than the window size would cause a single window's data to span multiple RocksDB segments, degrading read performance.

An IllegalArgumentException is thrown if these constraints are violated.

Javadoc for `segmentInterval`

The only added parameter is segmentInterval. The Javadoc is adapted from the existing Stores.persistentVersionedKeyValueStore parameter

java

For the new overloads, the existing note about retentionPeriod is replaced by a note about segmentInterval, since changing retentionPeriod alone no longer impacts the underlying storage format when segmentInterval is set explicitly:

java


Proposed Changes

The changes are minimal because the internal plumbing already supports a configurable segment interval.

  1. Stores.java : Add the new overloads listed above. Each delegates to the existing private persistentWindowStore(...) method (or equivalent), passing the user-provided segmentInterval instead of the computed default. Add validation as specified.
  2. RocksDbSessionBytesStoreSupplier.java: add a constructor overload that accepts an explicit segmentInterval and adapt segmentIntervalMs() to return the segmentInterval set
  3. No changes needed to:
    1. WindowBytesStoreSupplier interface — already defines segmentIntervalMs()
    2. SessionBytesStoreSupplier interface — already defines segmentIntervalMs()
    3. RocksDbWindowBytesStoreSupplier — already accepts segmentInterval in its constructor
    4. AbstractSegments, CachingWindowStore, WindowStoreBuilder — already consume segmentIntervalMs() from the supplier. No modifications required.
    5. BuiltInDslStoreSuppliers — the DSL path creates stores via Stores.* or internal supplier constructors, and does not need to expose segment interval (it is a low-level tuning parameter, not a DSL-level concern). Users who want to set it use Materialized.as(WindowBytesStoreSupplier) with a custom supplier.

Compatibility, Deprecation, and Migration Plan

  • Backward compatible All existing methods retain their current signatures and behavior. The new overloads are purely additive.

  • No deprecations

  • Migration. Users who currently instantiate internal suppliers directly (e.g., new RocksDbWindowBytesStoreSupplier(...)) to control segment interval can migrate to the new public API overloads.

  • State store compatibility. As noted in the Javadoc, changing the segment interval for an existing store requires clearing local state, since it changes the on-disk segment layout. This is the same constraint that already applies when retention changes today — the difference is that with this KIP, users can change retention without triggering a segment layout change.

Test Plan

  • Unit tests for each new Stores.* overload verifying:

    • Correct segment interval is passed through to the underlying supplier.

    • Validation rejects invalid values (below 60 seconds, smaller than window size for window stores).

    • Default behavior is preserved when using the existing overloads without segmentInterval.

  • Integration tests verifying that a window/session store created with a custom segment interval functions correctly (put, get, range queries, expiration/cleanup).

  • Test that changing retention without changing segment interval does not require a state store restore (the primary motivating use case).

Rejected Alternatives

NA

results.title: KIP-1367: Reserve apiKey values for private use

storage.value:
Status

Current state: Under discussion

Discussion thread: here

JIRA: here

Released: <Kafka Version>

Please keep the discussion on the mailing list rather than commenting on the wiki (wiki discussions get unwieldy fast).

Motivation

Message types in Kafka are keyed by a unique apiKey to uniquely identify them. These include all RPC types used by the brokers and controllers, metadata records stored in the KRaft metadata log and the data stored by coordinators.

Kafka contributors regularly introduce new message types in order to evolve the Kafka protocol. However, contributors run the risk of adopting an apiKey that is subsequently claimed by another proposal while they prototype their work. This is a problem shared by other Apache projects as well [0]

A workaround for this is for contributors to use a large value for apiKey which is currently unused and is unlikely to be used in the near future. apiKey is represented as a short with non-negative range from [0, 32767]. This KIP proposes formalising the reservation of the last 1024 values, i.e. [31744, 32767] for private use, ensuring future protocol changes would take the reserved values into account.

Public Interfaces

javaMessageGenerator typeClassGeneratorTypes, List messageClassGeneratorTypes, boolean allowCustom) throws Exception { // ... try (DirectoryStream directoryStream = Files.newDirectoryStream(Paths.get(inputDir), JSON_GLOB)) { for (Path inputPath : directoryStream) { try { MessageSpec spec = JSON_SERDE.readValue(inputPath.toFile(), MessageSpec.class); if (spec.isCustom() && !allowCustom) { throw new RuntimeException("Failed to process custom spec " + inputPath); } // ... } // ... } } // ... } }]]>


javaMessageSpec= CUSTOM_MIN_API_KEY; } }]]>


groovybuild.gradle



Proposed Changes

The change involves modifying MessageGenerator to accept a boolean flag --allow-custom which defaults to false. In addition, we add a new method, MessageSpec#isCustom which returns true if the apiKey is in the private reserved range.

MessageGenerator would only generate Java types for MessageSpecs with apiKey >= CUSTOM_MIN_API_KEY if --allow-custom is set to true and fail with a runtime exception otherwise.

The Gradle task processMessages is also modified to read a property allowCustomSpecs and pass --allow-custom flag appropriately.

Having this opt-in ensures that upstream PRs with a private spec inadvertently will result in the Gradle task failing.

Compatibility, Deprecation, and Migration Plan

The change is completely backwards compatible and incurs no cost to existing users. The range for apiKeys is quite large with about ~100 values being currently used. Reserving the last 1024 entries for private use should not cause any issues to existing users.

Test Plan

MessageGeneratorTest will be updated to ensure the correctness of --allow-custom

Documentation Plan

The documentation in Kafka Protocol section will be updated to note that the last 1024 values for apiKeys are reserved.

The change will also be mentioned in the release notes.

Rejected Alternatives


Using negative values

While this will work, it will make any future work that tries to transform the value into the negative space more involved.

results.title: KIP-1368: Client framework name and version

storage.value:
Status

Current state: Under discussion

Discussion thread: here

JIRA: here

Please keep the discussion on the mailing list rather than commenting on the wiki (wiki discussions get unwieldy fast).

Motivation

The Apache Kafka clients are often wrapped by frameworks such as Spring. Kafka does this itself in Kafka Streams and Kafka Connect. There is no architected way of identifying clients running within such frameworks which can hinder problem determination.

When diagnosing an issue from the client logs, the application code is not directly calling the Kafka client. This means there's a mismatch between what the application developer wrote and how the Kafka client is being used. Behaviors such as retries or transactions can be implemented in the framework rather than the application. Having the information about whether a framework is being used can illuminate why the application is appearing to behave in a particular way.

Proposed Changes

Three client configurations are added which can be set by frameworks embedding Kafka clients (producer, consumer and admin). The configurations are client framework name (the name of the framework), client framework version (the version of the framework) and client framework ID (additional framework-specific context which may not be relevant to all frameworks). These are flowed to the broker in the ApiVersions request alongside the client software name and version providing more comprehensive context information about clients wrapped by frameworks.

The values are set using the CommonClientConfigs.CLIENT_FRAMEWORK_NAME_CONFIG , CommonClientConfigs.CLIENT_FRAMEWORK_VERSION_CONFIG  and CommonClientConfigs.CLIENT_FRAMEWORK_ID_CONFIG  keys in the usual way. These configs are not intended to be set by regular applications. Kafka Connect and Kafka Streams both disallow setting these configuration properties and treat them as invalid configurations if set. If other frameworks provides a way for the application to set its own Kafka configs, they should also prevent the application from setting values for the client framework name, version and ID. 

The framework name should begin with the reversed Internet domain name for the framework owner, followed by the framework's name. For a framework such as Spring, the framework name would be chosen by Spring and the framework version would reflect the version of Spring.

For Kafka's own frameworks, Kafka Streams and Kafka Connect, Apache Kafka automatically sets the configs as follows:


Kafka StreamsKafka Connect
client.framework.name org.apache.kafka.streams org.apache.kafka.connect 
client.framework.version Kafka client version, such as 4.5.0 Kafka client version, such as 4.5.0 
client.framework.id Logical identifier used to group connections for the same Kafka Streams instance (process id)Connect worker ID

For example, let’s say that Kafka Streams is using the producer in Apache Kafka 4.5.0. It would set the following configurations:

  • "client.framework.name" = "org.apache.kafka.streams"

  • "client.framework.version" = "4.5.0"

  • "client.framework.id" = "F0DDEDA5-C8C6-493A-B026-F38A13C4E4D8"  (the Kafka Streams process id)

Then, in ApiVersions request, the following fields would be set:

  • ClientSoftwareName: "apache-kafka-java"

  • ClientSoftwareVersion: "4.5.0"

  • ClientFrameworkName: "org.apache.kafka.streams"

  • ClientFrameworkVersion: "4.5.0"

  • ClientFrameworkId: "F0DDEDA5-C8C6-493A-B026-F38A13C4E4D8" 

Here's an example of Kafka Connect configurations:

  • "client.framework.name" = "org.apache.kafka.connect"

  • "client.framework.version" = "4.5.0"

  • "client.framework.id" = "192.168.86.66:8083"

The framework ID in this case is the Connect worker ID.

Metrics

Kafka brokers today do collect metrics for client connections (see o.a.k.common.network.Selector ) and connections are counted by each <clientSoftwareName, clientSoftwareVersion>  pair, with a limit of 100 keys. The potential cardinality increase if we also key by client framework name and version could be significant, so these metrics are not augmented with client framework information.

KIP-714 introduced client metrics observability in the brokers. The client matching selectors are augmented by the addition of three new selectors:

  • client_framework_name  - client framework name.
  • client_framework_version  - client framework version.
  • client_framework_id  - client framework ID.

These new selectors can be included in the match  configuration property of client-metrics resources, and can also be specified on the kafka-client-metrics.sh  tool in the --match  option, such as the following which registers a client-metrics resource to collect consumer metrics for all Kafka Streams clients:

shell

The broker metrics plugin will also add client_framework_name , client_framework_version  and client_framework_id  labels for clients which provide this information in their ApiVersions request. This is the natural extension of KIP-714 with this new client information.

Public Interfaces

Kafka protocol

ApiVersions RPC

Tagged fields are added to the most recent version of the ApiVersions RPC request, which is v6 (introduced in Apache Kafka 4.5 as part of KIP-1313).

Request schema

The KIP adds three tagged fields to v6. The maximum length of each of the new fields is 249 characters (see KIP-1233), and the request will fail with INVALID_REQUEST  if the length is exceeded.

Starting with Apache Kafka 5.0, the broker will also enforce the maximum length of 249 characters to both the client software name and client software version.

Response schema

The v6 response schema is unchanged.

Client API changes

ClientTelemetryContext

The org.apache.kafka.server.telemetry.ClientTelemetryContext  interface is augmented with methods to provide the client telemetry exporter a proper way of obtaining the information it needs to add resource labels to the metrics pushed by the clients. Only the new methods are shown below. Note that the principal is mentioned in KIP-714 as one of the broker-added resource labels, but that is already available to the exporter via the AuthorizableRequestContext  and it is not replicated here.

java clientFrameworkName(); /** * Returns the client framework version for the client request, if known. * * @return the client framework version for the corresponding {@code PushTelemetryRequest} API call */  Optional clientFrameworkVersion(); /** * Returns the client framework ID for the client request, if known. * * @return the client framework ID for the corresponding {@code PushTelemetryRequest} API call */ Optional clientFrameworkId(); /** * Returns the client connection's source address for the client request. * * @return the client connection's source address for the corresponding {@code PushTelemetryRequest} API call */  String clientSourceAddress(); /** * Returns the client connection's source port for the client request. * * @return the client connection's source port for the corresponding {@code PushTelemetryRequest} API call */  int clientSourcePort(); /** * Returns the receiving broker's node ID for the client request. * * @return the receiving broker's node ID for the corresponding {@code PushTelemetryRequest} API call */ int nodeId(); }]]>

Configuration

Client configuration

The configuration keys are defined in org.apache.kafka.clients.CommonClientConfigs  as CommonClientConfigs.CLIENT_FRAMEWORK_NAME_CONFIG , CommonClientConfigs.CLIENT_FRAMEWORK_VERSION_CONFIG  and CommonClientConfigs.CLIENT_FRAMEWORK_ID_CONFIG . The maximum length of these configs is 249 characters.

ConfigurationDescriptionValues
client.framework.name For a client embedded in a framework, the name of the framework. User applications should not set this configuration directly. Importance: LOWType: STRING, default: null. If specified, must match the regular expression ”[a-zA-Z0-9](?:[a-zA-Z0-9\\-.]*[a-zA-Z0-9])?"
client.framework.version For a client embedded in a framework, the version of the framework. User applications should not set this configuration directly. Importance: LOW

Type: STRING, default: null. If specified, must match the regular expression ”[a-zA-Z0-9](?:[a-zA-Z0-9\\-.]*[a-zA-Z0-9])?"

client.framework.id For a client embedded in a framework, an optional framework-specific ID. User applications should not set this configuration directly. Importance: LOW

Type: STRING, default: null. If specified, must match the regular expression ”(?:[A-Za-z0-9\\-._~+]|%[0-9A-Fa-f]{2})+"

Client metrics configuration

The valid values for the match configuration property of client metrics resources are augmented by this KIP.

ConfigurationDescriptionValue
match The match criteria for selecting which clients the subscription matches. If a client matches all of these criteria, the client matches the subscription.

A list of key-value pairs.

The valid keys are:

  • client_instance_id - client instance ID.
  • client_id  - client ID.
  • client_framework_id  - client framework ID.
  • client_framework_name  - client framework name.
  • client_framework_version  - client framework version.
  • client_software_name  - client software implementation name.
  • client_software_version  - client software implementation version.
  • client_source_address  - client connection's source address from the broker's point of view.
  • client_source_port  - client connection's source port from the broker's point of view.

The values are anchored regular expressions.

Metrics

Broker-added resources labels for client metrics

Building on KIP-714, the following new labels should be added by the broker metrics plugin as metrics are received.

Label nameDescription
client_framework_idThe client's framework ID as reported in ApiVersionsRequest.
client_framework_nameThe client's framework name as reported in ApiVersionsRequest.
client_framework_versionThe client's framework version as reported in ApiVersionsRequest.

Tools

kafka-client-metrics.sh

The set of valid keys in the --match option is augmented by the addition of client_framework_id , client_framework_name  and client_framework_version .

Compatibility, Deprecation, and Migration Plan

No impact on existing users.

Test Plan

Unit tests will be added.

Rejected Alternatives

None considered.

results.title: KIP-1369: API-Contract Annotations for Nullity/Thread Safety

storage.value:
Status

Current state: Draft

Discussion thread: here

JIRA: ASF JIRA5aa69414-a9e9-3523-82ec-879b028fb15bKAFKA-20833

Motivation

Kafka's null-safety and thread-safety contracts live only in Javadoc, so nothing enforces them. A method that starts returning null, or a field read without its lock, compiles clean and breaks at runtime. Concurrency is also affected: Kafka is heavily threaded, and the lock-ownership reasoning behind many classes lives only in javadoc.

This proposal annotates Kafka's public API with existing contract annotations. A typed @Nullable or @GuardedBy("lock") beats a Javadoc sentence: it is uniform, greppable, shows in the IDE and generated docs, and tools read it without parsing prose. These concepts are already duplicated across the ecosystem, so rather than issue Kafka's own we can reuse the CLASS-retained SpotBugs and JSR-305 annotations, which the build's existing tools already recognise.

Public Interfaces

Kafka annotates its public API with existing annotations, added compileOnly via spotbugs-annotations (which also brings jsr305). All are @Retention(CLASS): read by build tooling and dropped by the JVM, so there is no runtime footprint. compileOnly keeps the jars out of the shadow jar and the published runtime dependencies.

Null-safety

edu.umd.cs.findbugs.annotations.@Nullable and @NonNull, applied where a value can be null:


java


These are SpotBugs' own annotations, so SpotBugs recognizes them directly, and IntelliJ, Kotlin, and NullAway recognize them too. They are CLASS-retained, so unlike javax.annotation.@Nullable (RUNTIME) they leave no dangling reference in shipped bytecode (JSpecify has this known limitation). For non-null-by-default a package may add @ReturnValuesAreNonnullByDefault or @DefaultAnnotation(NonNull.class) from the same jar.

Thread-safety

javax.annotation.concurrent.@GuardedBy, @Immutable, @ThreadSafe, @NotThreadSafe


java { ... } @NotThreadSafe public class KafkaConsumer { ... } final class ConsumerNetworkThread { @GuardedBy("this") private boolean running; }]]>


@GuardedBy is in Error Prone's recognized set, so if Kafka ever adds Error Prone its GuardedBy checker verifies lock discipline with no upstream change.

Proposed Changes

Enforcement

SpotBugs (already in the check phase) recognizes the nullness annotations, so they are checked with no new setup. Flow-sensitive checks (a @Nullable dereferenced unchecked, or a @GuardedBy lock actually held) need Error Prone or the Checker Framework and are out of scope; both already recognize these annotations, so adopting them later needs no upstream change. -Werror is unaffected: the annotations add no javac warnings.

Checkstyle keeps the vocabulary consistent, with no new tooling. Each module's import-control.xml allows edu.umd.cs.findbugs.annotations and javax.annotation.concurrent, and disallows the rest of javax.annotation; most-specific-match means the concurrency package stays allowed while the RUNTIME-retained javax.annotation.@Nullable/@Nonnull are banned, so nullness always uses the CLASS-retained findbugs types.

Rollout

Pilot clients, package by package, starting with the consumer and producer public API. spotbugs-annotations is added compileOnly to clients (it is already compileOnly in several server-side modules). Generated generator classes wait until the generator emits annotations.

Set the non-null default per package with @DefaultAnnotation(NonNull.class) in package-info.java, rather than on individual classes, so a package opts in as a unit. Expect a cleanup pass: the default surfaces every field, return, and parameter that is actually nullable, each of which then gets an explicit @Nullable.

Compatibility

Additive and compile-time only: no runtime behavior, wire format, or signature changes. The annotations are CLASS-retained and their jars are compileOnly, so nothing reaches a consumer's runtime classpath or the shadow jar. jsr305 (pulled compileOnly via spotbugs-annotations) is Apache-2.0 and already resolves transitively in the build.

ScenarioBehavior
Existing Java consumerNo change; annotations are invisible at runtime.
Contributor in IntelliJNullness inspections fire; IntelliJ recognizes these annotations by default.
Kotlin consumerKotlin reads the CLASS-retained findbugs nullness annotations from the compiled bytecode and infers nullability
Scala consumerScala 2.13 does not read nullability annotations; no change.

Test Plan

  • SpotBugs flags a dereferenced @Nullable and a violated @NonNull
  • Checkstyle rejects an import of javax.annotation.Nullable and allows javax.annotation.concurrent
  • the annotations render in generated Javadoc
  • no spotbugs-annotations/jsr305 classes appear in the clients shadow jar or runtime classpath
  • clients consumer/producer public API compiles clean under -Werror once annotated
  • existing build and tests pass

Rejected Alternatives

Define Kafka-owned annotations. Custom @Nullable/@GuardedBy/etc. under org.apache.kafka.common.annotation (the KIP-1265 pattern) was considered. Rejected because these concepts are already duplicated across JSR-305, SpotBugs, the Checker Framework, and Error Prone; a Kafka set is one more duplicate that tools would not recognize without extra work (SpotBugs by name, Error Prone only via an upstream PR). Reusing the existing CLASS-retained annotations is less code and immediately recognized.

JSpecify. The modern nullness standard, but @Retention(RUNTIME): as compileOnly it leaves a dangling reference in shipped bytecode, and it covers nullness only, not thread-safety. The CLASS-retained findbugs annotations avoid the residue and pair with the javax.annotation.concurrent set.

javax.annotation.@Nullable for nullness. It matches the thread-safety package, but is @Retention(RUNTIME), so it leaves the dangling reference the CLASS-retained findbugs @Nullable avoids.

Do nothing. The status quo that left KAFKA-9234 open since 2019.

Relationship to Other KIPs

KIPRelationship
Created Kafka-owned annotations for API audience; this reuses existing annotations for API contracts, since nullness and concurrency are already standardized.

ASF JIRA5aa69414-a9e9-3523-82ec-879b028fb15bKAFKA-9234

Original request from 2019

results.title: KIP-1370: Include Instance and Rack IDs in kafka-streams-groups.sh Member Output

storage.value:
Status

Current state: Under Discussion

Discussion thread: here

JIRA: ASF JIRA5aa69414-a9e9-3523-82ec-879b028fb15bKAFKA-20888, ASF JIRA5aa69414-a9e9-3523-82ec-879b028fb15bKAFKA-20883


Motivation

KIP-1071 (https://cwiki.apache.org/confluence/pages/viewpage.action?pageId=393677857) introduced Streams groups, the StreamsGroupDescribe API, and the  kafka-streams-groups.sh command-line tool.

The StreamsGroupDescribe response and the corresponding Admin API representation already expose the optional instance ID and rack ID of each Streams group member. However, kafka-streams-groups.sh --describe --members does not currently display either field.


The instance ID identifies a static group member and remains stable when the member restarts. Displaying it is useful for mapping dynamically generated member IDs to application instances and for diagnosing static membership issues. The rack ID is primarily useful when investigating rack-aware task placement. Since it is optional and is generally needed only for detailed diagnostics, it should be included only in verbose member output.


This KIP proposes the following behavior:

  • The GROUP-INSTANCE-ID column will be displayed when --members is specified only if at least one group member has instance ID.
  • The rack ID is displayed only when --members and --verbose are specified together.

  This also makes verbose member output an additive extension of the regular member output: information available in the regular output, including the instance ID, is not omitted when verbose output is requested.

Public Interfaces

This KIP introduces no new command-line options and does not change any public Java API, network protocol, configuration, metric,  or persisted data format.

It changes the human-readable output of the existing kafka-streams-groups.sh --describe --members command by adding member instance and rack information. Although console tool output is not considered a formal public interface under the Kafka KIP process, the output changes are documented in this KIP because they are user-visible and may affect scripts that parse the command output.

Proposed Changes

The member output of kafka-streams-groups.sh will expose the instance ID and rack ID already available in StreamsGroupMemberDescription.

CommandGROUP-INSTANCE-IDRACK-ID
--describe --membersIncludedNot included
--describe --members --verboseIncludedIncluded


The column order will change as follows:

CommandFromTo

--describe --members

(at least one group member has instance Id. non-empty string)

GROUP → MEMBER → PROCESS → CLIENT-ID → ASSIGNMENTS


 

GROUP → MEMBER → GROUP-INSTANCE-ID → PROCESS → CLIENT-ID → ASSIGNMENTS

--describe --members

GROUP → MEMBER → PROCESS → CLIENT-ID → ASSIGNMENTS

--describe --members --verbose

(at least one group member has instance Id. non-empty string)

GROUP → TARGET-ASSIGNMENT-EPOCH → TOPOLOGY-EPOCH → 

MEMBER → MEMBER-PROTOCOL → MEMBER-EPOCH → PROCESS →

CLIENT-ID → ASSIGNMENTS


 

GROUP → TARGET-ASSIGNMENT-EPOCH → TOPOLOGY-EPOCH → 

MEMBER → GROUP-INSTANCE-ID → MEMBER-PROTOCOL → MEMBER-EPOCH

→ PROCESS → CLIENT-ID → RACK-ID → ASSIGNMENTS

--describe --members --verbose

GROUP → TARGET-ASSIGNMENT-EPOCH → TOPOLOGY-EPOCH → 

MEMBER → MEMBER-PROTOCOL → MEMBER-EPOCH → PROCESS

→ CLIENT-ID → RACK-ID → ASSIGNMENTS

 

The instance ID will be displayed whenever --members is specified. The rack ID will only be displayed when --members and --verbose are specified together.

Instance IDs and rack IDs will be rendered as follows:

Source ValueConsole output
null or Optional.empty()-
Empty String ("")-
Non-empty stringThe value as reported

Although a null protocol value is converted to Optional.empty() by the Admin client, an empty string may be represented as a present optional value. The command will treat both cases as an unavailable value to avoid producing an empty table column. All other columns and their ordering will remain unchanged. The implementation will use the existing StreamsGroupMemberDescription#instanceId() and StreamsGroupMemberDescription#rackId() methods. No Admin API or protocol changes are required.


Compatibility, Deprecation, and Migration Plan

This change does not affect the Admin API, network protocol, broker or client configurations, or persisted data formats. No broker or Kafka Streams client migration is required.

The only user-visible impact is the addition of columns to the human-readable member output:

  • --describe --members adds GROUP-INSTANCE-ID.
  • --describe --members --verbose adds GROUP-INSTANCE-ID and RACK-ID.

Users or scripts that rely on fixed column positions may need to update their parsing logic after upgrading the command-line tool. No deprecation period or special migration tool is required. The new output format will take effect when the updated kafka-streams-groups.sh is used; older versions of the tool will continue to produce the previous format. The previous output layout will not be retained as a separate mode.


Test Plan

The existing kafka-streams-groups.sh tests will be extended to verify that:

  • --describe --members includes GROUP-INSTANCE-ID only when at least one member has instance ID information, and does not include RACK-ID.
  • --describe --members --verbose includes GROUP-INSTANCE-ID under the same condition and includes RACK-ID.
  • GROUP-INSTANCE-ID is omitted when none of the group members has instance ID information.
  • Non-empty instance IDs and rack IDs match the corresponding Streams group member metadata.

  • Both null values, represented as Optional.empty(), and empty strings ("") are rendered as -. (If it is possible for empty strings)

  • Existing columns, assignments, and other describe modes remain unchanged.

The existing Streams group command test suite will continue to validate that listing, state, offsets, topology, and other member output behavior is not affected.

Integration tests will verify the command output with actual group metadata, while command-level unit tests will cover absent and empty-string values.


Rejected Alternatives

Include both IDs only in verbose output

This was rejected because the instance ID represents the stable identity of a static member and should be available in the regular member view.

Include the rack ID in non-verbose output

This was rejected because rack information is optional and primarily useful for detailed assignment diagnostics. Including it by default would unnecessarily widen the regular member output.

results.title: Design notes

ancestors.title: KIP-1289 Support Transactional Acknowledgments for Share Groups

storage.value:
This document contains some rough design notes about how to support transactional acknowledgements for share groups.

Application programming interface

Prior to KIP-1289, applications chose how to acknowledge record delivery using the share.acknowledgement.mode consumer configuration. It seems to me that neither implicit  nor explicit  is really ideal. I propose that we introduce a third acknowledgement mode transactional . This gives a nice clean way to enforce correct API usage in the application.

Transactional acknowledgement mode has the following features:

  • Acknowledgements are explicit, meaning that every record received from poll(Duration)  must be acknowledged using ShareConsumer.acknowledge(...)  before the next call to poll(Duration) .
  • ShareConsumer.commitSync(...)  and ShareConsumer.commitAsync(...)  are not permitted. The acknowledgements are committed as part of a transaction so these specific methods are not appropriate.
  • ShareConsumer.setAcknowledgementCommitCallback(...)  is likewise not permitted. The acknowledgements will be completed once the transaction commits so the callback is not as useful as it is with asynchronous, non-transactional acknowledgements.
  • AcknowledgeMode.RENEW  is not permitted. It is incompatible with transactions.

The following code snippet shows how the application code might look.

java producer = new KafkaProducer(prodProps); ShareConsumer shareConsumer = new KafkaShareConsumer(consumerProps) { producer.initTransactions(); producer.setShareGroupTransactionAdapter(shareConsumer); shareConsumer.subscribe(Set.of("INPUT")); ConsumerRecords recs = shareConsumer.poll(Duration.ofMillis(10000)); for (ConsumerRecord rec : recs) { producer.beginTransaction(); producer.send(new ProducerRecord("OUTPUT", 0, rec.key(), rec.value()); shareConsumer.acknowledge(rec); producer.commitTransaction(); } }]]>

We need to define some kind of bridge between the producer and the share consumer so that shareConsumer.acknowledge(rec)  results in a transactional request to be sent to the share-partition leader. This is the purpose of producer.setShareGroupTransactionAdapter() . The internal details need to be ironed out, but this gives quite clean application code (there's no Producer.sendShareGroupAcknowledgementsToTransaction()  or equivalent for example).

Kafka protocol

To fit in with the current protocol design, I think we need 2 (or perhaps 3, depending on taste) new RPCs. They are:

  • TxnShareAcknowledge - sent by the client to the share-partition leader - the transactional equivalent of ShareAcknowledge
  • ShareTxnComplete - sent by the share coordinator to the share-partition leader at transaction completion so the record states in the share partition can be updated
  • TxnWriteShareGroupState - sent by the share-partition leader to the share coordinator - we could perhaps make these extra fields on the regular WriteShareGroupState RPC

TxnShareAcknowledge

Here's the request schema.

java

Note that the Gap acknowledge type is applied directly to the share partition state. Any of Accept, Release and Reject can be acknowledged transactionally. Generally Accept will be used, but a transactional application might conceivably want to release or reject as part of its transaction. The Renew acknowledge type is not supported.

ShareTxnComplete

java

TxnWriteShareGroupState

The delivery state reflects the state if the transaction commits. So, for an Accept acknowledgement, it will be Acked (2). For a release acknowledgement, it will be Available (0). For a reject acknowledgement, it will be Archiving (3) or Archived (4), depending upon whether the record will be written to the dead-letter queue.

If the transaction rolls back, the delivery state will return to Available and the delivery count will be unchanged (not decremented by the rollback).

java

ReadShareGroupState

It will be necessary to read transactional state. Here's the updated response schema.

For a transactional state, the transactional ID, producer ID and producer epoch will be provided. The delivery state will be the state if the transaction commits. If the transaction rolls back, the record will return to the Available state, and will be subject to the usual delivery count checks to determine whether it should be archived. The delivery count will be the value whether the transaction commits or rolls back.

java

Feature enablement

It will be necessary to introduce a new share.version  to enable this support (3). It seems that there is no need to have a new transaction.version  because there is no change to the protocol or records for the transaction coordinator. The transactions will include the __share_group_state  topic in much the way that transactions include the __consumer_offsets  topic when offsets are committed transactionally. But in both cases, the transaction coordinator is not really aware of the nuances of the behaviour of these topics, just that partitions have been registered in the transaction and transaction markers must be written at transaction completion.

results.title: Aegis MCP Governance Gateway Proposal

storage.value:
This is the proposal for entry into the Apache Incubator, formatted for the Incubator cwiki. Aegis is a working codename; a name search will be run and the ASF trademark process followed if the project is accepted. The document follows the ASF Incubator proposal template and states the maturity of the code honestly, including what is implemented and what is deferred to the roadmap.

Proposal metadata

FieldValue
Proposal nameAegis MCP Governance Gateway (codename)
Proposed short nameaegis (subject to name search)
Proposal dateto be set at submission
SponsorApache Incubator PMC
ChampionGreg Stein
MentorsLarry McCay (Apache Knox); additional IPMC mentors being recruited by the Champion
Initial codeJava 21 multi-module reference implementation, 36 Maven modules, 347 tests passing
Reference repositoryhttps://github.com/vaquarkhan/aegis-mcp-gateway (public, Apache-2.0)
LicenseApache License 2.0
Discussion listgeneral at incubator.apache.org

Abstract

Aegis MCP Governance Gateway is a vendor-neutral, secure-by-default Model Context Protocol (MCP) gateway that puts one governed, auditable control plane in front of many Apache data and streaming engines, so an AI agent never talks to Flink, Kafka, Spark, or Iceberg directly. Every agent action passes one fail-closed governance chain: secure-by-default tool exposure, per-caller authentication and scope, a policy decision point, approval for destructive operations, egress and server-side request forgery defense, rate limiting, circuit breaking, prompt-injection screening, output bounding and redaction, tool-catalog integrity, and a tamper-evident hash-chained audit trail. Engines plug in through a small service provider interface and contribute only tool definitions and backend calls.

Proposal

We propose to develop, under Apache governance, a Layer 7 policy MCP gateway plus a family of engine adapters. A proxy forwards bytes and a router dispatches by capability, but neither is a trust boundary. A gateway is: it knows the tool, the principal, the budget, and the policy for every call, and it can deny, redact, gate, and record. The gateway core is stateless at the protocol edge so it can scale behind an ordinary load balancer once shared governance state is externalized. It aligns with OAuth 2.1 and OpenTelemetry today, and treats SPIFFE, SLSA, and the AI-governance frameworks (NIST AI Risk Management Framework, ISO/IEC 42001) as alignment goals to reach as the roadmap items land, not as claims of current compliance. The initial contribution is a working Java reference implementation: a reusable gateway core, four in-depth engine adapters (Flink, Kafka, Spark, Iceberg), and a further set of thinner adapters for the wider Apache data platform. During incubation the priorities are community building, IP clearance, and promoting the roadmap items to full implementations.

Background

The Model Context Protocol has become a common way for AI agents to reach tools and data. As organizations connect agents to distributed Apache data estates, an agent that needs Flink, Kafka, Spark, and Iceberg must either drive each engine control plane directly or connect to a sprawl of independent, mostly read-only MCP servers, each with its own security posture, no shared audit, and no unified policy. An MCP server that can reach a control plane (a JobManager REST API, a Kafka AdminClient, a SQL gateway, an Iceberg catalog) is a privileged client. Shipping one safely is effectively shipping an access-control product: authentication, authorization, approval for destructive actions, redaction of secrets and personal data, rate and cost limits, and forensic audit. Many existing options lack these controls and carry single-maintainer sustainability risk. A single governed gateway, developed in the open under neutral governance, gives the ecosystem a shared standard for how agents operate Apache systems safely.

Rationale

A single governed gateway resolves the problems of the decentralized approach:

  • Security. One place enforces identity, authorization, approval, redaction, egress, and audit, instead of each server reimplementing or omitting them.
  • Maintainability. Adding an engine is a small adapter, not a new security model. There is one chain to review and harden, so the security review surface stays flat as engines are added.
  • Governance. One control plane for policy, budget, and provenance, with a stable deny taxonomy so operators can alert on codes such as POLICY_DENIED or APPROVAL_REQUIRED across every engine with one rule.

Doing this under Apache governance keeps it neutral across vendors and engines rather than leaving agent access to fragmented single-vendor servers.

Initial goals

  1. Establish the project and practice the Apache Way: transparency, consensus, meritocracy, and community over code.
  2. Complete IP clearance for the existing code and land it under Apache-2.0 with correct LICENSE and NOTICE files.
  3. Publish and stabilize the adapter service provider interface so per-engine adapters are small, reviewable contributions.
  4. Promote the roadmap items to full implementations: externalized high-availability state, CIMD and SPIFFE identity, a full Cedar runtime, vault-backed credential exchange, and an OpenTelemetry SDK bridge.
  5. Produce the first Apache source releases and grow a diverse, multi-organization contributor base.

Current status

Aegis is a new codebase with a working multi-module reference implementation. The design, threat model, low-level design, and standards research are complete and public. The code builds green and is tested. A published design-conformance matrix maps every design claim to Done or Roadmap, so the maturity line is explicit.

Verified build and test state

  • 36 Maven modules: a gateway core, adapters for 33 Apache engines (four in-depth today, Flink, Kafka, Spark, and Iceberg, and 29 thinner integrations covering Cassandra, HBase, Hive, Pulsar, Airflow, NiFi, Druid, Pinot, Doris, Impala, Calcite, Hudi, Paimon, Kudu, Ignite, BookKeeper, Ozone, Hadoop, ZooKeeper, Solr, Superset, Arrow Flight, Beam, Storm, Flume, ActiveMQ, CouchDB, Ranger, and Atlas), and a shaded runnable distribution. These are engine adapters the gateway supports, which is distinct from external adopters.
  • Builds with JDK 21 and runs on JDK 17 or newer with Maven 3.9 or newer.
  • 347 unit and integration tests across all modules, all passing, zero failures and zero errors on a clean build.

Implemented in 0.1.0

  • The governance chain with ordered steps and first-denial-wins semantics.
  • Identity: shared bearer and a hashed multi-caller token file with per-caller scope, and an OAuth 2.1 resource-server mode with JWKS validation. Constant-time secret comparison and fail-closed startup validation.
  • Approvals: HMAC-SHA256 signed, TTL-bounded, single-use, tool-and-scope-bound tokens with replay rejection.
  • Policy: a builtin decision point, a live fail-closed OPA HTTP decision point, and a Cedar-style deny-file or HTTP delegate.
  • Per-caller outbound credential pass-through so a downstream engine can see a per-caller Authorization value when one was bound at admission.
  • Egress and server-side request forgery defense: allow list plus unconditional deny of cloud metadata and non-routable ranges, including numeric IP encodings and resolved addresses, with redirects disabled on outbound clients.
  • Rate limiting, circuit breaking, per-tool timeout, read-only SQL guard, identifier validation, output bounding, and data-loss-prevention redaction.
  • Tool-catalog integrity with durable pins and a fail-closed switch, a tamper-evident hash-chained audit, Prometheus metrics, and GenAI-shaped span log lines.
  • Two transports: stdio and authenticated Streamable HTTP with TLS, plus health, readiness, and metrics endpoints. A CycloneDX software bill of materials is produced at build time.

Deferred to the roadmap (honestly labeled, not sold as implemented)

  • A full Cedar policy runtime, and vault-backed or token-exchange credential resolution.
  • Externalized high-availability state (shared nonce, rate, and audit stores). Until then, run a single replica; multi-replica replay protection and rate limits require the shared store.
  • The MCP Tasks extension for long-running jobs, an OpenTelemetry SDK bridge, a full Merkle and signature-based reconciliation proof, and true semantic routing and caching.

These are tracked in the roadmap and the design-conformance matrix that ship with the code.

Community

The repository is public and is no longer a single-author project. As of this writing it has four contributors with merged code: the initial author plus three others, including PJ Fanning, an established contributor active across multiple Apache projects. There are merged pull requests from several external contributors and further open pull requests under review (adapter tests and an SPI extension), alongside forks and open issues. Governance oversight is forming: Greg Stein (Champion) and Larry McCay (mentor) join the initial author to form a PPMC of three, which already meets the quorum to vote on releases and invite further members. The author is embedded in the communities the project draws from (Spark, Iceberg, Kafka, Burr) and maintains MCP-related packages with more than 350 thousand downloads, so there is an existing user base to draw contributors from. Growing this into a diverse, multi-organization community is the purpose of incubation.

Known risks

Orphaned products

Low to moderate. Agentic access to data systems is a growing need and the governance gap is real, so demand is unlikely to vanish. The initial author has maintained open-source projects since 2013 rather than abandoning them, and the MCP-related packages already have a real user base, which lowers the abandonment risk. Mitigation: build a multi-organization community, keep the core small and standards aligned, and keep adapters independent so the project survives the departure of any single contributor.

Inexperience with open source

Low. The initial author has about 23 years in software, has worked in open source since 2013, and has contributed to Apache Spark, Apache Iceberg, Apache Kafka, Apache Burr ,Spring AI agentcore , JSR368  and other projects, so the norms of public development, code review, and releases are familiar. Mentors will still help with the ASF-specific mechanics of voting, board reports, and IP clearance, which are process details rather than a gap in open-source experience.

Homogenous developers

The project already has a small but active community and a forming governance structure. There are four contributors with merged code, There are merged pull requests from several external contributors, an open PR from a further contributor extending the adapter SPI, forks, and open issues under review. Governance oversight is in place: Greg Stein (ASF Member and Director) is the Champion, and Larry McCay (Apache Knox) has agreed to mentor and join the PPMC. The honest remaining gap is diversity of affiliation: the committers so far are not yet spread across enough independent organizations. That is a growth goal, not a blocker, and it is the main thing incubation is meant to build. Mitigation: recruit committers from more than one organization before graduation, keep the adapter contract small so per-engine contributions are natural, and use good-first-issue and adapter-sized work to onboard newcomers.

Reliance on salaried developers

Low current reliance; the work to date is largely independent. The project will attract contributors with varied motivations and employers so no single company can stall it.

Relationships with other Apache products

Aegis consumes the public interfaces of Flink, Kafka, Spark, Iceberg, and other Apache data systems and does not fork or modify them. Aegis is itself a governed MCP server: its adapters reach each engine's public control plane and expose a governed tool surface, so the value is the shared governance chain across many engines rather than a new per-engine tool set. Aegis is not proposed for any engine core, and we will coordinate with the relevant engine communities on the dev lists.

Apache Knox (https://knox.apache.org/) deserves specific mention. Knox is a Layer 7 security gateway for Hadoop and data-ecosystem services, with a mature provider chain for authentication, federation, identity assertion, authorization, and audit, and a Knox committer has offered to mentor this project. Aegis is not a replacement for Knox and does not intend to duplicate it. Knox governs HTTP and REST access to services; Aegis governs the MCP tool-call layer an AI agent uses, including secure-by-default tool exposure, approval for destructive actions, tool-catalog integrity, prompt-injection screening, and the MCP transports themselves. The two operate at different layers and can align. Knox's RFC 8693 token exchange with an actor-chain principal model and its externalized token state map directly onto the Aegis credential and high-availability roadmap, and we intend to coordinate with Knox early rather than re-derive that work.

Excessive fascination with the Apache brand

The project seeks Apache governance for its community model and neutrality, not for the brand. Until and unless accepted, it uses a neutral name and does not use the Apache marks or the feather. The breadth of engine adapters reflects a common governance surface, not an attempt to claim the ecosystem; only four adapters are in-depth today and the rest are explicitly thin. We are open to trimming or quarantining the thin adapter set for the initial contribution if the community prefers a smaller, sharper surface during bootstrap; the governance core, not the adapter count, is the point.

Documentation

Public documentation exists and will be maintained in the repository: an end-to-end design with architecture decision records, a low-level design with architecture, sequence, and state diagrams, a threat and governance model, a design-conformance matrix, standards research, and operations and adapter guides.

Initial source

The initial source is the Java multi-module gateway described above, in a public repository at https://github.com/vaquarkhan/aegis-mcp-gateway under the initial author, so the Champion, mentors, and prospective reviewers can read the code before any vote. It includes the gateway core, the four in-depth adapters, the thinner adapters, the shaded distribution, runnable examples, and the documentation set. On acceptance it will be donated under a Software Grant.

Source and intellectual property submission plan

The initial author will submit the code under a Software Grant Agreement and complete IP clearance early in incubation, with ICLAs from every committer. The repository is Apache-2.0 licensed and source files carry author attribution today; the standard Apache-2.0 source-file header will be applied, and the LICENSE and NOTICE files will be finalized at that time.

The author asserts authorship and the right to contribute the work, and will confirm provenance and authorship during IP clearance so the grant is clean. A self-run provenance and license scan (SCANOSS plus a Maven dependency-license inventory) has already been performed and is published in the repository; it found no Category X license and no third-party code requiring removal. We raise this proactively so the IPMC can review it rather than discover it. Because Aegis is a security-focused project, an independent security review of the governance-critical code (identity, approval, egress and request-forgery defense, and the interceptor chain) is planned during incubation; a license scan establishes provenance, not security, and we do not conflate the two.

External dependencies

Runtime dependencies are Apache-2.0 or compatible, including the MCP Java SDK, a servlet container for the HTTP transport, SLF4J, Logback, and Nimbus for JOSE and JWT, with JUnit for tests. Per-engine adapters add that engine to the official client, for example the Kafka clients library. A full dependency review and a CycloneDX software bill of materials are produced. No GPL or ASF category X dependency is introduced into the core.

Cryptography

Aegis uses standard, library-based cryptography: HMAC-SHA256 for approval tokens, TLS for the HTTP transport, and JSON Web Token validation for OAuth. Signature-based integrity is an optional gate. The project will comply with ASF export notification requirements.
